b: Simple definition# A consistency model is a promise about what a read can return after writes, when data is copied across machines. Strong models behave like a single copy. Weaker models allow stale or reordered reads in exchange for latency and availability. The problem# Replicas live on different machines and in different regions, and messages between them are delayed or lost. A customer transfers money and immediately sees the old balance. Two people book the same seat. Two regions accept conflicting updates. The real question is which anomalies your use case can tolerate. &ldquo;Is it consistent?&rdquo; is too vague to answer. The consistency spectrum# From strongest to weakest (simplified) flowchart LR L[&#34;Linearizable&lt;br/&gt;single-copy, real-time order&#34;] --&gt; S[&#34;Sequential&lt;br/&gt;one global order&#34;] --&gt; C[&#34;Causal&lt;br/&gt;cause before effect&#34;] --&gt; SESS[&#34;Session guarantees&lt;br/&gt;read-your-writes, monotonic&#34;] --&gt; E[&#34;Eventual&lt;br/&gt;replicas converge&#34;] Model Guarantee Example use Linearizable Every operation appears to happen instantly between its call and return; all clients see the same order Account balance limits, leader election, locks, unique usernames Sequential A single total order consistent with each client&rsquo;s program order Some replicated logs Causal If A could have caused B, everyone sees A before B Comments and replies, chat, collaborative edits Read-your-writes You always see your own updates User profile updates Monotonic reads You never see older data after newer data Feeds, dashboards Eventual If writes stop, replicas converge Counters, recommendations, caches, read models Key conceptConsistency is per operation, not per system A banking app needs linearizable checks for &ldquo;is the balance enough?&rdquo;, read-your-writes for &ldquo;my profile&rdquo; and eventual consistency for &ldquo;spending insights&rdquo;. Pick per use case. CAP, stated correctly# CAP (Brewer, proven by Gilbert and Lynch): when a network Partition happens, a replicated system must choose between Consistency (linearizability) and Availability (every non-failed node answers). It is not &ldquo;pick two of three&rdquo;. Partitions are not optional, so the choice is only C or A during a partition. CP systems (etcd, ZooKeeper, Spanner, CockroachDB, Kafka with min.insync.replicas) refuse some requests rather than return wrong data. AP systems (Cassandra and DynamoDB in some configurations, DNS, caches) answer with possibly stale data and reconcile later. PACELC: the everyday trade-off# PACELC (Abadi): if there is a Partition, choose A or C; Else, in normal operation, choose Latency or Consistency. System (typical config) P → E → Spanner, CockroachDB C C (pays latency for consensus) Cassandra, DynamoDB (eventual reads) A L MongoDB (majority writes and reads) C C PostgreSQL + async replicas C on the primary L for replica reads (stale) The &ldquo;else&rdquo; part matters more day to day: strong consistency across regions costs round-trips. Quorums# With N replicas, write to W and read from R. If R + W &gt; N, every read overlaps the latest write. N W R Effect 3 2 2 Strong-ish reads; tolerates 1 failure 3 3 1 Fast reads, fragile writes 3 1 1 Fast and available, eventually consistent Quorums alone are not full linearizability (concurrent writes, sloppy quorums, clock-based conflict resolution). Consensus protocols close those gaps. Consensus: Raft in one picture# Consensus lets a group of nodes agree on an ordered log despite failures. Raft is the most widely used protocol (etcd, Kafka KRaft, CockroachDB, TiKV, Consul). Raft: leader replicates a log entry to a majority sequenceDiagram participant C as Client participant L as Leader (term 5) participant F1 as Follower 1 participant F2 as Follower 2 C-&gt;&gt;L: write x=1 L-&gt;&gt;F1: AppendEntries(index 42, x=1) L-&gt;&gt;F2: AppendEntries(index 42, x=1) F1--&gt;&gt;L: ok L-&gt;&gt;L: majority (2 of 3) has it, so commit index 42 L--&gt;&gt;C: success L-&gt;&gt;F2: (F2 catches up later) Leader election uses randomised timeouts and terms. A node needs votes from a majority. A majority (quorum) must store an entry before it is committed. Use 3 or 5 nodes, which tolerate 1 or 2 failures. A minority partition cannot commit, which is the CP behaviour. Time, clocks and ordering# Wall clocks drift, so &ldquo;last write wins&rdquo; by timestamp can silently lose updates. Logical clocks (Lamport) order events; vector clocks detect concurrency. Hybrid logical clocks (HLC) combine physical time with logical counters (used by CockroachDB and YugabyteDB). TrueTime (Spanner) exposes bounded clock uncertainty and waits it out to give external consistency. In event-driven systems, prefer per-entity version numbers and partition ordering over timestamps. Isolation levels: consistency inside a database# Level Prevents Still allows Read committed Dirty reads Non-repeatable reads, lost updates, write skew Repeatable read / snapshot isolation The above plus non-repeatable reads Write skew (two doctors both go off call) Serializable (SSI or 2PL) All of the above Nothing, at a performance cost For money movement, use serializable, or explicit locking or constraints (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, unique keys, check constraints) on the rows that protect invariants. Conflict resolution under eventual consistency# Last-writer-wins is simple but lossy. CRDTs (conflict-free replicated data types: counters, sets, maps) merge automatically and deterministically. They suit collaborative and offline-first apps. Application merge: keep both versions and resolve them with business rules or a human. Choosing: a simple guide# If you need… Choose An invariant that must never be violated (balance ≥ 0, unique IBAN) Linearizable or serializable inside one consensus or ACID boundary A user to see their own change immediately Read-your-writes (route to the leader, or use session tokens) Global low-latency reads of slowly changing data

b: This path takes you from the event log to a secure, regulated, end-to-end platform design. Each step builds on the previous one. The case studies at the end of each module combine what you have learned into a complete design.
d: Every article in a deliberate order: Kafka and event-driven design, consistency and sagas, data platforms and governance, then threat modelling, security, AI security and regulation. About three weeks at one to two hours a day.

b: Simple definition# A data platform collects data from operational systems, stores it reliably and cheaply, and turns it into trusted data products for reporting, analytics, machine learning and AI. The modern default is a lakehouse: open table formats on object storage, queried by many engines under one governance catalog. The problem# Operational databases are built for transactions, not for analysis across years and systems. Historically, companies copied data into warehouses (fast and governed but expensive and closed) and lakes (cheap and flexible but often a &ldquo;data swamp&rdquo;). The duplication brought inconsistent numbers, high cost and a separate security model per copy. Warehouse vs lake vs lakehouse# Data warehouse Data lake Lakehouse Storage Proprietary, managed Files on object storage Open table formats on object storage Data Structured Any Any, with tables on top Transactions Yes No Yes (ACID via table format) Engines One Many, ungoverned Many, through one catalog Strength BI performance, governance Cost, ML, raw data Both, without copies Open table formats# A table format adds database features to files: ACID commits, schema evolution, time travel, partition evolution and row-level updates. Apache Iceberg Delta Lake Apache Hudi Origin Netflix → Apache Databricks → Linux Foundation Uber → Apache Strength Engine-neutral, hidden partitioning, REST catalog standard Deep Spark and Databricks integration Upserts and incremental processing Ecosystem (2026) Broadest multi-vendor support (Snowflake, AWS S3 Tables, BigQuery, Databricks, Trino, Flink, Spark, DuckDB) Databricks, Fabric, with UniForm Iceberg compatibility Streaming-heavy upsert workloads Iceberg format v3 (spec finalised in 2025, with engine support rolling out through 2026) adds: Deletion vectors: compact bitmaps in Puffin files that mark deleted rows, so updates and deletes are faster. Row lineage: a stable row ID and a last-updated sequence number per row, for incremental processing and CDC. The VARIANT type for semi-structured data; geometry and geography types; nanosecond timestamps; default column values; and multi-argument transforms. How an Iceberg table works flowchart TB CAT[&#34;Catalog&lt;br/&gt;table → current metadata pointer&#34;] --&gt; META[&#34;metadata.json&lt;br/&gt;schema, partition spec, snapshots&#34;] META --&gt; ML[&#34;manifest list&lt;br/&gt;(one per snapshot)&#34;] ML --&gt; M1[&#34;manifest&lt;br/&gt;data files + stats&#34;] ML --&gt; M2[&#34;manifest&#34;] M1 --&gt; F1[&#34;Parquet data files&#34;] M1 --&gt; DV[&#34;deletion vectors (v3)&#34;] A commit atomically swaps the catalog pointer to new metadata. Readers see a consistent snapshot, and time travel reads older snapshots. Catalogs: the control point# The catalog tracks tables and, increasingly, enforces governance for every engine. Iceberg REST Catalog is the open API standard used by most engines. Apache Polaris is an open-source Iceberg REST catalog, originally from Snowflake. Unity Catalog (open-sourced by Databricks) covers tables, volumes, models and functions, with access control and lineage. AWS Glue / S3 Tables, Google BigLake and Microsoft OneLake are cloud catalogs. Key conceptGovern in the catalog, not per engine When Spark, Trino, Flink, Snowflake and Python all read the same Iceberg table through one catalog, access policies, masking and lineage can be enforced once. See data security. Medallion layers# Governed lakehouse: medallion layers on Iceberg · drawn with Archify · zoom, guided views, search and SVG/PNG export. Open full screen ↗ Layer Content Rules Bronze (raw) Data as received from CDC, events and files; append-only Keep the source fidelity; add ingestion metadata; restricted access Silver (conformed) Cleaned, de-duplicated, typed, joined to reference data; PII tokenised Quality checks; standard keys and types Gold (products) Business-level aggregates and data products (customer 360, daily positions, regulatory datasets) Contracts, SLOs, owners, documentation Ingestion: batch, CDC and streaming# CDC (Debezium, cloud DMS, Fivetran, Airbyte) from OLTP databases into bronze. Streaming: Kafka → Flink, or Kafka Connect Iceberg sink → Iceberg, with commits every few seconds to minutes. This is a &ldquo;streaming lakehouse&rdquo;. Batch files and APIs for partner and legacy data. Zero-ETL integrations (operational DB → warehouse or lakehouse managed by the cloud) reduce pipeline code. Check what transformations and governance you lose. Orchestrate with Apache Airflow 3, Dagster or cloud equivalents; transform with dbt or SQLMesh, or Spark and Flink jobs. Query and serving engines# Need Engines Large transformations Apache Spark, Flink (batch mode), dbt on a warehouse Interactive SQL Trino / Starburst, Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks SQL, Dremio Local and embedded analytics DuckDB Real-time OLAP (sub-second on fresh data) Apache Pinot, ClickHouse, Apache Druid, StarRocks ML and AI Spark ML, Ray, feature stores (Feast), vector search Data mesh and data products# Data mesh (Zhamak Dehghani) has four principles: Domain ownership: the payments domain owns payments data. Data as a product: discoverable, addressable, trustworthy, self-describing, interoperable, secure. Self-serve data platform: a platform team provides the lakehouse, catalog, pipelines and governance as a service. Federated computational governance: global rules (classification, interoperability, privacy) automated in the platform; domains decide locally. A data product bundles data, code, metadata, a contract, SLOs, an owner and access policies. Most enterprises adopt a hybrid: a central platform with domain-owned data products. Data platforms for AI# Unstructured data (documents, emails, call transcripts) is governed in the same catalog: volumes, document tables, embeddings. Feature stores give consistent features for training and serving. Vector search inside the lakehouse or in a vector database, with the same access policies as the source documents.

b: Simple definition# Apache Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform. At its core it is a replicated, partitioned, append-only log: producers append records, the cluster stores them durably for a configured time, and any number of consumers read them independently. Each consumer can re-read old records whenever it needs to. The problem it solves# Point-to-point integration between N systems creates up to N×(N−1) connections, each with its own format, retry logic and failure modes. Traditional message queues delete a message once it is consumed, so a new consumer cannot replay history. Kafka gives every producer and consumer one durable, ordered, replayable stream per topic. It scales to millions of events per second. Core concepts# Concept What it is Record (event) Key, value, headers and timestamp. The key decides the partition and therefore the ordering. Topic A named stream of records, for example payments.authorised.v1. Partition An ordered, append-only log. A topic is split into partitions for parallelism. Ordering is guaranteed only within a partition. Offset The position of a record in a partition. Consumers track how far they have read with offsets. Broker A server that stores partitions and serves reads and writes. Replica / leader / follower Each partition has N replicas on different brokers. One is the leader, which handles reads and writes, and the others follow. ISR The in-sync replicas: followers that are caught up with the leader. Controller (KRaft) Manages cluster metadata (topics, partitions, leaders) using a Raft quorum. Consumer group Consumers that share the work. Each partition is assigned to exactly one member. Share group Queue-style consumption. Many consumers can read from the same partition, and each record is acknowledged on its own. Apache Kafka 4.x cluster architecture · drawn with Archify · zoom, guided views, search and SVG/PNG export. Open full screen ↗ Partitions, keys and ordering# The key decides the partition; ordering holds per partition flowchart LR P[&#34;Producer&#34;] --&gt;|&#34;key = account-42&#34;| H{&#34;hash(key) mod 6&#34;} H --&gt; P0[&#34;partition 0&#34;] H --&gt; P3[&#34;partition 3&lt;br/&gt;all account-42 events, in order&#34;] H --&gt; P5[&#34;partition 5&#34;] Records with the same key always go to the same partition, so they stay in order. For example, every event for account-42 is processed in sequence. Hot keys create hot partitions. A single huge merchant or tenant can overload one partition, so choose keys with high cardinality and even load. The number of partitions caps consumer parallelism within a group. You can add partitions later, but that changes the key-to-partition mapping for new records and breaks per-key ordering across the change. Plan for it up front. Replication and durability# Each partition is replicated (replication.factor=3 is the production norm) across brokers placed in different racks or availability zones. Write path with acks=all and min.insync.replicas=2 sequenceDiagram participant Pr as Producer participant L as Leader (broker 1) participant F1 as Follower (broker 2) participant F2 as Follower (broker 3) Pr-&gt;&gt;L: produce(batch), acks=all L-&gt;&gt;L: append to local log F1-&gt;&gt;L: fetch F2-&gt;&gt;L: fetch L--&gt;&gt;Pr: ack once ISR has the batch (ISR size at least 2) Setting Meaning Typical production value replication.factor Copies of each partition 3 min.insync.replicas Minimum ISR size for a write with acks=all to succeed 2 acks (producer) 0 none, 1 leader only, all full ISR all (the default since Kafka 3.0) unclean.leader.election.enable Allow an out-of-sync replica to become leader, which can lose data false With RF=3 and min.insync.replicas=2, the cluster survives one broker failure without losing acknowledged writes and without stopping writes. If two replicas are lost, writes fail rather than risk data loss. That is the right trade-off for financial data. KRaft: Kafka without ZooKeeper# Older Kafka versions stored metadata in Apache ZooKeeper. KRaft (Kafka Raft) moves metadata into Kafka itself: a small quorum of controller nodes keeps a replicated metadata log. Kafka 4.0 (March 2025) removed ZooKeeper entirely. Clusters must run in KRaft mode, and you migrate from ZooKeeper while on 3.x. It is simpler to operate (one system), fails over faster and supports far more partitions per cluster. Run 3 controllers (or 5 for very large clusters). Use dedicated controller nodes in production; combined broker-and-controller mode is for small or dev clusters. Dynamic controller quorums (KIP-853) let you add or remove controllers without downtime. Reading: consumer groups and share groups# Consumer groups are the classic model. Partitions are split among the group members, each member reads its partitions in order, and the group commits offsets to the internal __consumer_offsets topic. That gives ordering and scale. But one slow record blocks its partition, and parallelism is capped at the partition count. The next-generation rebalance protocol (KIP-848), GA in Kafka 4.0, moves partition assignment to the broker-side group coordinator. Members join and leave incrementally, without stop-the-world rebalances. Enable it with group.protocol=consumer. Share groups (Queues for Kafka, KIP-932) reached GA in Kafka 4.2 (2026). They provide queue semantics on top of topics: Many consumers can process records from the same partition concurrently, so parallelism is not limited by the partition count. Each record is acquired with a time-limited lock and individually acknowledged (ACCEPT, RELEASE to retry or REJECT). The broker counts delivery attempts, which enables poison-message handling. Kafka 4.2 adds a RENEW acknowledgement to extend a lock for slow processing, plus share-partition lag metrics. Use them for work queues (jobs, notifications, tasks) where per-key ordering does not matter. Keep consumer groups for ordered stream processing. Consumer group Share group Unit of assignment Partition

b: Answers are short, just enough to check your understanding. Each section links to the articles with the full explanations. TipHow to use this page Cover the answer, explain it in your own words, then compare. Mark anything you hesitated on and reread the linked article. Aim for 80% before moving on. 1. Kafka fundamentals# Read: Kafka architecture. What is a Kafka partition? An ordered, append-only log. Topics are split into partitions for parallelism, and ordering holds only within one partition. What decides which partition a record goes to? The record key, hashed by the partitioner. The same key always maps to the same partition, unless the partition count changes. What is the ISR? The in-sync replicas: replicas fully caught up with the leader. Only these count towards acks=all. What do RF=3 and min.insync.replicas=2 protect against? Losing one broker without losing acknowledged writes and without stopping writes. Why disable unclean leader election? It can elect an out-of-sync replica and silently lose acknowledged data. What replaced ZooKeeper, and since when exclusively? KRaft controllers (a Raft metadata quorum), exclusively since Kafka 4.0. What do share groups add? Queue semantics: many consumers per partition, per-record acknowledgement, delivery counting. GA in Kafka 4.2. What does a compacted topic keep? At least the latest record per key. Tombstones (null values) delete keys. What is tiered storage for? Cheap long retention, by moving older segments to object storage. 2. Producers, consumers and guarantees# Read: Producers, consumers &amp; exactly-once. At-most-once vs at-least-once? At-most-once commits before processing, so events can be lost. At-least-once commits after processing, so events can be duplicated. What does the idempotent producer do? De-duplicates producer retries using a producer ID and sequence numbers. What do Kafka transactions make atomic? Writes to multiple partitions plus consumer offset commits. Does Kafka exactly-once cover a write to PostgreSQL? No. Use an idempotent consumer, or the outbox pattern. What happens if processing exceeds max.poll.interval.ms? The consumer is considered failed, and its partitions are rebalanced to other members. What is a dead-letter topic? Where records that fail permanently go, with error details, so the stream keeps moving. What does KIP-848 change? Rebalancing becomes broker-coordinated and incremental (group.protocol=consumer), avoiding stop-the-world rebalances. 3. Event-driven architecture and contracts# Read: Event-driven architecture and Schemas &amp; event contracts. Event vs command? An event is a past fact for unknown consumers. A command asks a specific receiver to act. What is event-carried state transfer? Events carry the data consumers need, so consumers do not call back to the producer. When orchestrate instead of choreograph? For multi-step business processes with compensation, SLAs and audit needs. What fields should every event have? A unique ID, type and version, source, event time, subject or key, and correlation and trace IDs. What does BACKWARD compatibility mean? New consumers can read data written with the previous schema, so you upgrade consumers first. How do you make a breaking schema change? Publish a new major-version topic, run v1 and v2 in parallel, migrate consumers, then retire v1. What does a data contract include beyond the schema? Semantics, quality rules, SLOs, ownership, classification and policies. 4. Stream processing# Read: Stream processing. Event time vs processing time? When the event happened, versus when the processor sees it. Use event time for correct business results. What is a watermark? An estimate that no events older than T remain, which lets windows close. Tumbling vs hopping vs session windows? Tumbling windows are fixed and non-overlapping. Hopping windows are fixed and overlapping. Session windows are bounded by inactivity gaps. How does Flink recover state? From the latest checkpoint (a consistent snapshot of state plus source offsets). When choose Kafka Streams over Flink? For Kafka-to-Kafka processing embedded in a microservice, with no separate cluster. What did Flink 2.2 add for AI? ML_PREDICT model inference and VECTOR_SEARCH in Flink SQL. 5. Consistency and transactions# Read: Consistency &amp; consensus and Distributed transactions. What does CAP really say? During a network partition, a replicated system must choose between consistency and availability. What does PACELC add? Without a partition, there is still a latency versus consistency trade-off. R + W &gt; N means what? Read and write quorums overlap, so reads see the latest acknowledged write. How many Raft nodes, and why? 3 or 5. A majority is needed, and odd sizes maximise tolerated failures. What anomaly does snapshot isolation allow? Write skew. What is the dual-write problem? Updating two systems without a shared transaction, so one can succeed while the other fails. Why avoid 2PC across microservices? It blocks on coordinator failure, adds latency, lowers availability, couples services, and many systems do not support it. What is TCC? Try (reserve, with expiry), then Confirm or Cancel. 6. Outbox, sagas, CQRS and event sourcing# Read: Outbox, CDC &amp; idempotency, Saga and CQRS &amp; event sourcing. How does the outbox pattern work? Write the state change and the event row in one local transaction, then relay outbox rows to the broker (polling or CDC). Why prefer log-based CDC as the relay? Low latency, low database load and commit-order preservation. How do you make a consumer idempotent? Record the event ID in the same transaction as the business change, or apply versioned, naturally idempotent updates. What is a compensating transaction? A new business action that semantically undoes an earlier saga step. What is a pivot step? The point of no return. Later steps must be retried until they succeed. Which ACID property do sagas lack? Isolation. Mitigate with semantic locks, commutative

b: Simple definition# Threat modelling is a structured way to answer: what are we building, what can go wrong, what are we going to do about it, and did we do a good job? It finds design-level security and privacy problems early, when fixing them is cheap. The problem# Scanners and pentests find implementation bugs late. They do not tell you that the design lets a support agent export every customer&rsquo;s data, or that the AI assistant can be tricked into calling the payments tool. Those are architecture flaws, and finding them in production is expensive or catastrophic. The four questions (Threat Modeling Manifesto)# What are we working on? Build a model: a data flow diagram (DFD), assets and trust boundaries. What can go wrong? Identify threats with STRIDE, attack trees, ATT&amp;CK and so on. What are we going to do about it? Mitigate, eliminate, transfer or accept. Did we do a good enough job? Validate with tests, reviews and pentests, and keep the model updated. Threat modelling workflow · drawn with Archify · zoom, guided views, search and SVG/PNG export. Open full screen ↗ Step 1: the data flow diagram# Element Symbol Examples External entity Rectangle Customer, partner bank, card network Process Circle Payment API, fraud service, AI agent Data store Parallel lines Ledger DB, Kafka topic, vector store Data flow Arrow HTTPS request, Kafka event, tool call Trust boundary Dashed line Internet/DMZ, service mesh, PCI zone, tenant boundary, model provider Simple DFD with trust boundaries flowchart LR U[&#34;Customer&lt;br/&gt;(external)&#34;] --&gt;|&#34;HTTPS + OAuth&#34;| GW subgraph DMZ[&#34;Trust boundary: edge&#34;] GW[&#34;API gateway&#34;] end subgraph CORE[&#34;Trust boundary: internal services&#34;] PAY((&#34;Payment service&#34;)) --&gt; DB[(&#34;Ledger DB&#34;)] PAY --&gt; K[(&#34;Kafka&#34;)] end GW --&gt;|&#34;mTLS&#34;| PAY PAY --&gt;|&#34;ISO 20022 over mTLS&#34;| SCHEME[&#34;Payment scheme&lt;br/&gt;(external)&#34;] TipThreats live on boundaries Most serious threats appear where data crosses a trust boundary. Spend your time there. Step 2: STRIDE per element# Threat Violates Example Typical mitigations Spoofing Authentication Stolen token used to call the payment API MFA, OAuth/OIDC, mTLS, workload identity Tampering Integrity Amount modified in transit or in Kafka TLS, signatures, MACs, immutable logs, input validation Repudiation Non-repudiation &ldquo;I never approved that transfer&rdquo; Signed audit logs, SCA evidence, timestamps Information disclosure Confidentiality IDOR exposes other customers&rsquo; statements Authorisation checks, encryption, masking, least privilege Denial of service Availability Bot floods the login or the LLM endpoint Rate limits, WAF, autoscaling, quotas, circuit breakers Elevation of privilege Authorisation Support role reaches admin functions RBAC/ABAC, least privilege, sandboxing, policy checks STRIDE-per-element: processes are subject to all six. Data stores to T, R (logs), I and D. Data flows to T, I and D. External entities to S and R. Other methods# Method Focus When to use PASTA Seven-stage, risk- and business-centric, attacker simulation High-value systems; aligns security with business impact LINDDUN Privacy threats: Linking, Identifying, Non-repudiation, Detecting, Data disclosure, Unawareness, Non-compliance Systems processing personal data (GDPR/DPDP DPIAs) Attack trees Goal at the root, ways to achieve it as branches Deep-dive on one critical asset (&ldquo;steal funds&rdquo;) MITRE ATT&amp;CK Real adversary tactics and techniques Detection engineering, red teaming, validating controls MITRE ATLAS Adversarial tactics against AI/ML systems AI and agent threat models Kill chain / Unified Kill Chain Attack stages SOC and incident response planning Step 3: rate and respond# Rating options: Likelihood × impact (High/Medium/Low) is simple and usually enough. CVSS v4.0 scores technical severity of vulnerabilities (not design risk). DREAD is older and subjective; use it with care. FAIR quantifies risk in financial terms (loss event frequency × loss magnitude), which suits risk committees. Responses: mitigate (add a control), eliminate (remove the feature or data), transfer (insurance, contract) or accept (an owner signs off, recorded in the risk register). Each mitigation becomes a backlog item with a test. Each acceptance gets an owner and a review date. Threat modelling AI and agent systems# Add these elements and threats to the DFD: Model (external or self-hosted), prompts (system and user), retrieved context (RAG), tools (MCP servers, APIs), memory, other agents. Threats: prompt injection (direct and indirect through documents and tool output), excessive agency, tool misuse, data leakage through outputs, memory poisoning, model or supply-chain compromise and unbounded consumption. Use the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025), the Top 10 for Agentic Applications (2026) and MITRE ATLAS as threat libraries. See AI security. Fitting it into delivery# When: at design (architecture review), for every significant change (a new trust boundary, data class or integration), and periodically for critical systems. Who: the team that builds it, plus a security champion or architect. Threat modelling is a team sport, not an outsourced document. How long: 60–90 minutes per feature-level session, iterated. Keep the model as code (Threat Dragon JSON, pytm, Threagile YAML) in the repo. Tools: OWASP Threat Dragon, Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool, pytm, Threagile, IriusRisk, ThreatModeler, and AI-assisted threat generation (always reviewed by humans). Evidence: regulators (DORA ICT risk management, RBI, PCI DSS 6.2 secure development) expect risk assessments of changes. Threat models provide them. Common mistakes# Common mistakeA one-off document for the audit Models go stale with the first change. Keep them in the repo and update them with design changes. Common mistakeBoiling the ocean Modelling the entire enterprise at once produces nothing
d: Finding design flaws before attackers do: the four-question framework, data flow diagrams and trust boundaries, STRIDE per element, PASTA, LINDDUN for privacy, attack trees, MITRE ATT&CK and ATLAS, risk rating with DREAD, CVSS and FAIR, threat modelling AI and agent systems, tools, and fitting it into agile delivery.

b: Simple definition# Data governance is the set of roles, policies, standards and tools that make sure data is known (catalogued and defined), trusted (good quality with traceable lineage), protected (secure and private) and used properly (meeting regulation and ethics) across its lifecycle. The problem# &ldquo;Why does the risk report say 4.2 billion and finance say 4.5?&rdquo; Two teams use different definitions of &ldquo;exposure&rdquo;, sourced from different copies, with no record of the transformations in between. Regulators require banks to prove where reported numbers come from. AI models trained on unknown data create legal and reputational risk. The operating model# Who does what flowchart TB COUNCIL[&#34;Data governance council&lt;br/&gt;policies, priorities&#34;] --&gt; CDO[&#34;CDO / data office&lt;br/&gt;standards, platform&#34;] CDO --&gt; OWN[&#34;Data owners (business)&lt;br/&gt;accountable per domain&#34;] OWN --&gt; STEW[&#34;Data stewards&lt;br/&gt;definitions, quality rules, issues&#34;] OWN --&gt; CUST[&#34;Data custodians (IT/platform)&lt;br/&gt;storage, security, operations&#34;] STEW --&gt; USERS[&#34;Data consumers&lt;br/&gt;use within policy&#34;] Role Accountability Data owner Business accountability for a data domain: who may access it, quality targets Data steward Definitions, glossary, quality rules, issue resolution Data custodian Technical operation: storage, backup, security controls Data product owner A data product&rsquo;s contract, SLOs and roadmap (data mesh) Reference frameworks include DAMA-DMBOK (the knowledge areas of data management) and the EDM Council DCAM / CDMC (capability models, including cloud data management controls). Metadata and the catalog# Metadata type Examples Technical Schemas, tables, columns, types, partitions Business Glossary terms (&ldquo;active customer&rdquo;), definitions, owners Operational Freshness, volumes, job runs, quality scores Security and privacy Classification (public, internal, confidential, restricted), PII tags, retention, legal basis Catalogs: platform catalogs (Unity Catalog, Polaris, AWS Glue / DataZone, Google Dataplex, Microsoft Purview) and enterprise catalogs (Collibra, Alation, Atlan, plus open-source DataHub and OpenMetadata). Automate harvesting; manual catalogs go stale. Lineage# Lineage shows where data came from and what happened to it, from source system to report or model. Column-level lineage is needed for regulatory reporting and impact analysis (&ldquo;if I change this column, which reports break?&rdquo;). OpenLineage (an LF AI &amp; Data project) is the open standard. Airflow, Spark, Flink, dbt and others emit run events; Marquez, DataHub and commercial catalogs collect them. Use lineage for impact analysis, root-cause analysis of bad numbers, privacy (where does PII flow?) and evidence for auditors. Data quality# Dimension Question Example check Completeness Is everything there? customer_id not null; row count within ±5% of yesterday Validity Does it follow the rules? IBAN format, currency in ISO 4217 Accuracy Does it match reality? Reconcile balances with the core banking ledger Consistency Does it agree across systems? Same customer status in CRM and core banking Uniqueness No duplicates? One row per payment_id Timeliness / freshness Is it recent enough? Gold table updated by 06:00 Tools: dbt tests, Great Expectations / GX, Soda, Deequ, and data observability platforms (Monte Carlo, Bigeye, and the observability features of the catalogs). Where to check: at ingestion (schema, contract), between layers (silver rules) and before publishing a gold product. Failing a critical check should stop publication, not just alert. Data contracts# Contracts are agreements between producers and consumers covering schema, semantics, quality, SLOs and ownership. They move quality upstream to the source team. See Schemas and event contracts for the ODCS format and CI enforcement. Master and reference data# Master data (customer, product, counterparty, legal entity) needs a golden record, built from matching and survivorship rules in MDM tools or a well-governed gold product. Reference data (currencies, country codes, LEIs, product hierarchies) must be versioned and shared centrally, not copied and edited per team. Regulatory reporting: BCBS 239# The Basel Committee&rsquo;s BCBS 239 principles for risk data aggregation and reporting require banks to have: strong governance and architecture accurate, complete, timely and adaptable risk data aggregation reports that are accurate, comprehensive, clear and timely, including under stress. In practice that means a lineage-backed, quality-controlled path from source to report, with owners and reconciliation. Supervisors (the ECB, the RBI and others) continue to flag gaps in BCBS 239 compliance, so treat it as a design requirement. Governance for AI# Know the provenance and rights of training and RAG data (consent, licences, legal basis). Track datasets → features → models → decisions lineage. Keep model cards and datasheets. Apply the same classification and access policies to embeddings and vector stores as to their source documents. The EU AI Act requires data governance for high-risk AI (training data quality, bias examination). See FinTech regulations. ISO/IEC 42001 provides an AI management system standard. Common mistakes# Common mistakeGovernance as a committee, not a capability Policies that are not automated in the platform are ignored. Encode classification, quality and access as code. Common mistakeA catalog nobody updates Manual documentation goes stale in weeks. Harvest metadata and lineage automatically. Common mistakeQuality checks only at the end Detecting problems in the gold report means the damage is done. Check at ingestion and between layers. Quick check# Data owner vs data steward? The owner is the business person accountable for a domain (access, quality targets). The steward manages definitions, quality rules and issues day to day. What is

b: How to use it# Use this checklist to review your own design before building, or a team&rsquo;s design at an architecture board. Score each area 0–3 and record the evidence. Ten review areas flowchart LR A1[&#34;1 · Goals &amp; NFRs&#34;] --&gt; A2[&#34;2 · Boundaries &amp; data ownership&#34;] --&gt; A3[&#34;3 · Events &amp; contracts&#34;] --&gt; A4[&#34;4 · Consistency&#34;] --&gt; A5[&#34;5 · Failure handling&#34;] A5 --&gt; A6[&#34;6 · Data platform &amp; governance&#34;] --&gt; A7[&#34;7 · Data security &amp; privacy&#34;] --&gt; A8[&#34;8 · Threats &amp; security&#34;] --&gt; A9[&#34;9 · AI risk&#34;] --&gt; A10[&#34;10 · Compliance &amp; operations&#34;] 1. Goals and non-functional requirements# Throughput (average and peak), latency budgets, availability, RPO and RTO stated per flow? Which flows are synchronous (the user waits) and which are asynchronous? Red flags: &ldquo;real-time&rdquo; undefined; no peak numbers; one SLO for everything. 2. Boundaries and data ownership# Each piece of data has one owning service? No shared databases between services? Do data that must change together live together? Red flags: services reading each other&rsquo;s tables; every change spans services. 3. Events and contracts# Events named as past-tense facts; integration events separated from internal ones? Keys chosen for ordering; partition count sized for growth? Schemas registered, compatibility mode chosen (transitive if replayed), CI checks in place? No secrets or unnecessary PII in events; trace context propagated? Red flags: schemaless JSON; compatibility NONE; low-cardinality keys; PAN in events. 4. Consistency# Consistency model stated per operation (strong where invariants live, eventual elsewhere)? Invariants protected inside one ACID or consensus boundary? Read-your-writes handled where users need it? Red flags: decisions made on async replicas or read models; &ldquo;eventually consistent&rdquo; used as an excuse. 5. Failure handling# Outbox (or equivalent) for state plus event; idempotent consumers; idempotency keys on APIs? Sagas with explicit compensations, timeouts and manual-review paths? Retries with backoff, DLTs, poison-message handling; the timeout (unknown) outcome designed? Reconciliation jobs for money and critical data? Red flags: @Transactional around remote calls; infinite retries; no compensation design. 6. Data platform and governance# Open table formats and one catalog; medallion or product layers defined? Owners, contracts and quality gates per data product; lineage captured automatically? Regulatory reports traceable to source (BCBS 239)? Red flags: copies per tool; no owners; quality checks only on final reports. 7. Data security and privacy# Data classified; sensitive identifiers tokenised early; masking by default? Encryption in transit and at rest with managed keys (HSM/KMS); key separation of duties? ABAC or row and column security; JIT access to restricted data; access recertification? Residency, retention and erasure (including immutable stores) designed? Red flags: production data in test; PII in logs and prompts; &ldquo;we encrypt the disk&rdquo; as the only control. 8. Threats and security architecture# Current threat model (DFD, trust boundaries, STRIDE, LINDDUN for personal data)? Zero trust: strong user and workload identity, mTLS, per-object authorisation? Supply chain: SBOM, signing, provenance, admission policy; secrets dynamic and short-lived? Crypto inventory and crypto-agility for PQC? Red flags: trusted internal network; authorisation only at the gateway; long-lived static credentials. 9. AI risk# AI use cases inventoried and classified (EU AI Act tier)? Least agency, user-scoped tools, human approval for consequential actions? Permission-aware RAG; output validation; token and cost limits? Red-teamed and continuously evaluated; traces kept? Red flags: agents with service-account superpowers; security rules only in the system prompt. 10. Compliance and operations# Applicable regulations listed (PCI DSS, DORA, PSD2/3, GDPR/DPDP, RBI, CERT-In, SEBI, AI Act); controls mapped once to many? Incident detection, classification and reporting clocks (4/6/24/72 h) automated and rehearsed? Resilience testing, restore tests, third-party register and exit plans? Monitoring: lag, DLTs, saga states, quality, access anomalies, cost? Red flags: compliance as an annual project; paper-only incident plans; unknown ICT dependencies. Scoring rubric# Score Meaning 0 Not considered 1 Considered, but not designed 2 Designed, but not yet verified 3 Designed and verified (tests, evidence, drills) A design is ready to build at an average of at least 2 with no zeros in areas 4, 5, 7 or 8. It is ready for production at 3 in all applicable areas. One-page review template# System: Reviewer: Date: Scope / flows reviewed: Scores: 1 Goals [ ] 2 Boundaries [ ] 3 Events [ ] 4 Consistency [ ] 5 Failure [ ] 6 Data/gov [ ] 7 Data sec [ ] 8 Security [ ] 9 AI [ ] 10 Compliance/ops [ ] Top 3 risks (with owner and due date): 1. 2. 3. Accepted risks (owner, review date): Decision: [ ] approve [ ] approve with conditions [ ] redesign Quick check# Which four areas must not score zero before building? Consistency, failure handling, data security and privacy, and threats and security. What does a score of 3 require? The area is designed and verified with evidence: tests, drills or audits.
d: A repeatable checklist for reviewing event-driven, data and security designs: ten review areas with questions and red flags, a 0–3 scoring rubric and a one-page review template.

b: Simple definition# A distributed transaction is an all-or-nothing update that spans more than one database or resource, for example debiting an account in one service and creating a shipment in another. The problem# Inside one database, ACID transactions are cheap and reliable. Microservices use database per service, and integrations add brokers and external APIs. Code like this: @Transactional public void placeOrder(Order o) { orderRepo.save(o); // DB 1 paymentClient.charge(o); // remote service, DB 2 kafkaTemplate.send(&#34;orders&#34;, o); // broker } …is not atomic. The charge may succeed while the DB commit fails, or the event may be sent for an order that rolls back. This is the dual-write problem. Two-phase commit (2PC)# Two-phase commit sequenceDiagram participant TC as Coordinator participant A as Resource A participant B as Resource B TC-&gt;&gt;A: PREPARE TC-&gt;&gt;B: PREPARE A--&gt;&gt;TC: YES (locks held, durable) B--&gt;&gt;TC: YES TC-&gt;&gt;TC: log COMMIT decision TC-&gt;&gt;A: COMMIT TC-&gt;&gt;B: COMMIT Prepare: each participant does the work, makes it durable, keeps its locks and votes yes or no. Commit or abort: the coordinator logs the decision and tells everyone. XA is the standard API for 2PC across databases and message brokers (JTA in Java). Why 2PC rarely fits microservices# Issue Effect Blocking If the coordinator dies after prepare, participants hold locks until it recovers (&ldquo;in doubt&rdquo;) Latency Extra round trips and fsyncs on every transaction Availability Every participant must be up, so availability multiplies down Coupling All services must share a transaction manager and support XA Support Many modern stores, cloud services, Kafka (for XA) and every REST API do not participate 2PC still has a place inside one platform: databases use it internally across shards, and some mainframe and messaging estates use XA. But do not stretch it across service boundaries. Option 1: avoid the distributed transaction# Often the best design is to redraw the boundary: If two pieces of data must always change together, they probably belong in one service, one aggregate and one database. Use a distributed SQL database (Google Spanner, CockroachDB, YugabyteDB, TiDB). It gives serializable ACID transactions across shards and regions using consensus plus 2PC internally, managed for you. You pay in write latency across regions. Option 2: local transaction + reliable event (outbox)# Commit the state change and the event in one local transaction, and publish the event asynchronously. Consumers react idempotently. See Outbox, CDC and idempotency. Option 3: saga# Split the business transaction into local transactions, each with a compensating action, coordinated by events (choreography) or by an orchestrator. See Saga pattern. Option 4: TCC and reservations# Try–Confirm–Cancel (TCC) reserves resources first and then confirms or cancels them: Try–Confirm–Cancel flowchart LR T[&#34;TRY&lt;br/&gt;reserve funds, hold seat&lt;br/&gt;(with expiry)&#34;] --&gt;|&#34;all tries OK&#34;| C[&#34;CONFIRM&lt;br/&gt;capture, ticket&#34;] T --&gt;|&#34;any try fails or timeout&#34;| X[&#34;CANCEL&lt;br/&gt;release holds&#34;] Card payments already work this way: authorise (hold) and later capture or void. Reservations expire automatically, so a crashed coordinator does not lock resources forever. Confirm and cancel must be idempotent, and cancel must handle &ldquo;try never arrived&rdquo; (an empty cancel). Comparison# Approach Consistency Coupling Availability Complexity Best for 2PC / XA Atomic High Lower Infrastructure Legacy estates, single platform Distributed SQL Serializable Shared DB High (consensus) Low for apps Data that truly belongs together Outbox + events Eventual Low High Medium Propagating state changes Saga Eventual, with compensation Low–medium High Medium–high Multi-step business processes TCC Eventual, with reservations Medium High High Inventory, seats, funds holds Designing for failure# Every remote call can succeed, fail or time out (unknown). Design the unknown case: query status, use idempotency keys, and reconcile. Make every step idempotent and retriable. Keep an audit log of steps and decisions. Run reconciliation jobs that compare systems and fix or flag drift. In finance this is mandatory, not optional. Common mistakes# Common mistake@Transactional around remote calls The annotation covers only the local database. Remote calls and broker sends are outside it. Common mistakeTreating a timeout as failure The remote side may have succeeded. Query, then decide; never assume. Common mistakeSplitting data that changes together If every change spans two services, the boundary is wrong. Merge them, or use a distributed SQL store. Quick check# What is the dual-write problem? Writing to two systems (for example a DB and a broker) without a shared transaction, so one write can succeed while the other fails. Why does 2PC block? Participants that voted yes must hold locks until they learn the decision. If the coordinator fails, they wait. What is TCC? Try–Confirm–Cancel: reserve resources tentatively (with expiry), then confirm all or cancel all. When is distributed SQL a good alternative? When the data truly belongs together and needs serializable transactions, and you can accept cross-region write latency. What three outcomes must every remote call handle? Success, failure and unknown (timeout). Summary# ACID does not span services. The dual-write problem is the root issue. 2PC and XA work but block, couple services and reduce availability, so avoid them across services. Prefer better boundaries, distributed SQL, the outbox, sagas or TCC reservations. Design for the unknown outcome with idempotency, status queries and reconciliation. References# Chris Richardson, Microservices patterns: Saga, Transactional outbox. Pat Helland, Life beyond Distributed Transactions. Google, Spanner: TrueTime and external consistency.
d: Why ACID across services is hard: how two-phase commit and XA work, why they rarely fit microservices, distributed SQL as an alternative, and the toolkit that replaces them: local transactions, outbox, idempotency, sagas, TCC and reservations.
t: Distributed Transactions: 2PC, XA and the Alternatives

b: Simple definition# A producer writes records to topic partitions. A consumer reads them and records its progress as offsets. Delivery guarantees describe what happens to a record when something fails in between: it can be lost, duplicated or processed exactly once. The problem# Networks drop acknowledgements, brokers fail over and consumers crash after doing work but before committing their offset. Without care you will lose events (a missed payment notification) or duplicate them (a double debit). You need to know which guarantee each flow needs and how to get it. The three delivery semantics# Semantics How it happens Risk Use for At most once Commit the offset before processing; no producer retries Loss Metrics where gaps do not matter At least once Process, then commit; producer retries Duplicates The default for most business events, with idempotent consumers Exactly once Idempotent producer + transactions + read_committed Complexity; Kafka-to-Kafka only Stream processing pipelines inside Kafka Key conceptEffectively-once is a design, not a setting Kafka&rsquo;s exactly-once covers reading from Kafka, processing and writing back to Kafka. When a side effect leaves Kafka (a database write, an email, a card network call), you get &ldquo;effectively once&rdquo; only with at-least-once delivery plus an idempotent consumer. See Outbox, CDC and idempotency. The producer# Producer internals flowchart LR APP[&#34;send(record)&#34;] --&gt; SER[&#34;Serialize&lt;br/&gt;key + value&#34;] --&gt; PART[&#34;Partitioner&lt;br/&gt;hash(key)&#34;] --&gt; ACC[&#34;Record accumulator&lt;br/&gt;batches per partition&#34;] --&gt; SENDER[&#34;Sender thread&lt;br/&gt;compress, send&#34;] --&gt; B[&#34;Leader broker&#34;] B --&gt;|&#34;ack / error&#34;| SENDER Important producer settings: Setting Recommendation Why acks all Durable against a leader failure enable.idempotence true (default since 3.0) The broker de-duplicates retries using producer ID + sequence number retries / delivery.timeout.ms High retries, bounded total timeout (for example 120 s) Retry transient errors without hanging forever max.in.flight.requests.per.connection ≤ 5 with idempotence Keeps ordering while pipelining linger.ms / batch.size 5–20 ms, 64–256 KB Bigger batches mean higher throughput compression.type zstd or lz4 Less network and disk use Transactions and exactly-once# A transactional producer (transactional.id) writes to several partitions and commits consumer offsets atomically. Downstream consumers with isolation.level=read_committed see only committed data. Exactly-once consume, process, produce in Kafka · drawn with Archify · zoom, guided views, search and SVG/PNG export. Open full screen ↗ Zombie fencing: a stable transactional.id plus an epoch means a restarted instance fences off an old &ldquo;zombie&rdquo; instance, which can no longer commit. Transactions version 2 (KIP-890, in the Kafka 4.x line) hardens the protocol against hanging transactions with server-side defences. Cost: a little extra latency (commit markers) and throughput overhead. Kafka Streams and Flink use this under the hood when you configure processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2 or the exactly-once sink mode. The consumer# Consumer loop (at-least-once) flowchart LR POLL[&#34;poll()&#34;] --&gt; PROC[&#34;process records&lt;br/&gt;(idempotently)&#34;] --&gt; COMMIT[&#34;commit offsets&lt;br/&gt;after success&#34;] --&gt; POLL PROC --&gt;|&#34;transient error&#34;| RETRY[&#34;retry with backoff&#34;] RETRY --&gt;|&#34;still failing&#34;| DLT[&#34;dead-letter topic&#34;] Offsets: turn off auto-commit for business processing (enable.auto.commit=false) and commit after the work succeeds. max.poll.interval.ms: if processing a batch takes longer than this, the consumer is evicted and its partitions rebalance. Keep batches small, or hand slow work to a share group or a worker pool. Rebalancing: prefer the new consumer protocol (group.protocol=consumer, KIP-848) for incremental, broker-coordinated assignment. With the classic protocol, use the cooperative-sticky assignor. Static membership (group.instance.id) avoids rebalances during rolling restarts. Lag (log-end offset minus committed offset) is the main health signal. Alert on lag growth and on time-based lag. Retries, dead letters and poison messages# Error type Handling Transient (timeout, 503) Retry with exponential backoff and jitter; then a retry topic for longer delays Permanent (validation, deserialisation) Send straight to a dead-letter topic (DLT) with error headers; alert; fix and replay Ordering-sensitive key Blocking retry, or park all later events for that key; do not skip ahead Share groups (Kafka 4.2) add broker-side delivery counts. A record that keeps failing can be REJECTed or sent to a dead-letter queue after N attempts, without custom retry topics. Example: Spring for Apache Kafka# @Configuration class KafkaConfig { @Bean DefaultErrorHandler errorHandler(KafkaTemplate&lt;String, Object&gt; template) { var recoverer = new DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer(template); // -&gt; payments.authorised.v1-dlt var backoff = new ExponentialBackOffWithMaxRetries(5); backoff.setInitialInterval(500); backoff.setMultiplier(2.0); var handler = new DefaultErrorHandler(recoverer, backoff); handler.addNotRetryableExceptions(ValidationException.class); // permanent: straight to DLT return handler; } } @Component class PaymentListener { private final ProcessedEventRepository processed; // idempotency store private final LedgerService ledger; @KafkaListener(topics = &#34;payments.authorised.v1&#34;, groupId = &#34;ledger-posting&#34;) @Transactional public void on(PaymentAuthorised event) { if (!processed.markIfNew(event.eventId())) return; // duplicate: already handled ledger.post(event); // same DB transaction as the marker } } The listener is at-least-once plus idempotent. The processed-event marker and the business update commit in one database transaction, so a redelivery after a crash is harmless.
d: Producing and consuming safely: batching and partitioning, idempotent producers, at-most-once vs at-least-once vs exactly-once, Kafka transactions and read_committed, offset management, rebalancing, retries, dead-letter topics and backpressure, with Spring for Apache Kafka examples.
h: Retries, dead letters and poison messages

b: Simple definition# Security architecture is the set of principles, patterns and controls that make a system resist, detect and recover from attacks by design. It covers identity, network, application, data, supply chain, cryptography and operations. Core principles# Principle Meaning Defence in depth Multiple independent layers, so one failure is not a breach Least privilege Minimum access, for minimum time Zero trust Never trust by network location; verify explicitly every time Secure by default Safe settings out of the box; insecure options require effort Fail securely Errors deny access. This is OWASP A10:2025, &ldquo;Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions&rdquo;. Assume breach Limit blast radius; detect and respond fast Separation of duties No single person or service can complete a critical action alone Economy of mechanism Simple designs are easier to verify Zero trust architecture# NIST SP 800-207 defines zero trust as moving defences from static network perimeters to users, assets and resources. Every request is authenticated, authorised and encrypted, based on identity and context. Zero trust: policy decision and enforcement flowchart LR SUBJ[&#34;User / workload&lt;br/&gt;+ device posture&#34;] --&gt; PEP[&#34;Policy enforcement point&lt;br/&gt;(gateway, mesh, ZTNA proxy)&#34;] PEP &lt;--&gt; PDP[&#34;Policy decision point&lt;br/&gt;identity, context, risk&#34;] PDP &lt;-.-&gt; SIG[&#34;Signals: IdP, EDR, threat intel,&lt;br/&gt;SIEM, data classification&#34;] PEP --&gt; RES[&#34;Resource&lt;br/&gt;(app, API, data)&#34;] Building blocks: Strong identity: phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2 passkeys) for people. Workload identity (SPIFFE/SPIRE, cloud workload identity, Kubernetes service accounts with OIDC federation) for services, with no long-lived secrets. Device posture (managed, patched, EDR running). Micro-segmentation: service mesh mTLS with authorisation policies, network policies, private endpoints. ZTNA replaces VPNs for user access to applications. Continuous evaluation: sessions re-evaluated on risk changes. The CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model (identity, devices, networks, applications and workloads, data) helps plan the journey. Application security: OWASP Top 10:2025# # Category (2025) Notes A01 Broken Access Control Still #1; now includes SSRF A02 Security Misconfiguration Cloud and framework defaults, verbose errors A03 Software Supply Chain Failures New/expanded: dependencies, build systems, distribution A04 Cryptographic Failures Weak or missing encryption, bad key handling A05 Injection SQL, NoSQL, OS command, LDAP, and template injection A06 Insecure Design Missing threat modelling and secure patterns A07 Authentication Failures Credential stuffing, weak sessions A08 Software or Data Integrity Failures Unsigned updates, insecure deserialisation A09 Security Logging and Alerting Failures Cannot detect or investigate A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions New: failing open, leaking errors, unsafe recovery Also use the OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023). Its top item, BOLA (broken object-level authorisation: changing /accounts/123 to /accounts/124), is the most common API breach cause. Check authorisation per object on every request. API security patterns: OAuth 2.0 / OIDC with short-lived tokens; FAPI 2.0 for financial APIs (sender-constrained tokens via mTLS or DPoP, PAR); schema validation at the gateway; rate limiting; no sensitive data in URLs; consistent error handling. Secure SDLC and DevSecOps# Security in the delivery pipeline flowchart LR D[&#34;Design&lt;br/&gt;threat model&#34;] --&gt; C[&#34;Code&lt;br/&gt;IDE checks, secrets scan&#34;] --&gt; B[&#34;Build&lt;br/&gt;SAST, SCA, SBOM&#34;] --&gt; T[&#34;Test&lt;br/&gt;DAST, API fuzzing&#34;] --&gt; R[&#34;Release&lt;br/&gt;sign, provenance, policy gate&#34;] --&gt; O[&#34;Operate&lt;br/&gt;runtime detection, patching&#34;] SAST (static analysis), SCA (dependency vulnerabilities and licences), secrets scanning, IaC scanning, container scanning, DAST and API testing. Frameworks: NIST SSDF (SP 800-218), OWASP SAMM, BSIMM. Security champions in each team; findings triaged by exploitability and reachability, not raw counts. Software supply chain security# Control What it does SBOM (CycloneDX, SPDX) Inventory of components for every artifact; feeds vulnerability response SLSA (v1.x) Build integrity levels: provenance, hardened build platforms Signing (Sigstore cosign, keyless with OIDC) Prove who built the artifact; verify at deploy Provenance attestations (in-toto) Prove how and from what source it was built Dependency hygiene Pinned versions, private mirrors, typosquatting checks, OpenSSF Scorecard Admission policy Only signed, attested, scanned images run (Kyverno, Gatekeeper) Regulation now pushes this: the EU Cyber Resilience Act (vulnerability reporting obligations from September 2026, full application from December 2027) and US federal secure software attestation requirements. Secrets management# No secrets in code, images or Git. Use Vault / OpenBao, cloud secret managers, or the External Secrets Operator. Prefer dynamic, short-lived credentials (database credentials issued per session) and workload identity federation over static keys. Rotate automatically; detect leaks with pre-commit hooks and repository scanning. Cryptography and post-quantum readiness# Use vetted libraries and modern defaults: TLS 1.3, AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305, Ed25519 or ECDSA P-256, SHA-256+, Argon2id or bcrypt for passwords. Post-quantum cryptography (PQC): NIST published FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA) and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA) in August 2024, and selected HQC as a backup KEM in 2025. The threat is &ldquo;harvest now, decrypt later&rdquo; for long-lived secrets, which is exactly what financial data is. What to do now: Build a cryptographic inventory (CBOM). Design crypto-agility (algorithms configurable, not hard-coded). Adopt hybrid key exchange (X25519 + ML-KEM) in TLS where supported; major browsers and CDNs already use
d: The core of enterprise security architecture: defence in depth and zero trust (NIST SP 800-207), identity for people and workloads, OWASP Top 10:2025 and API security, secure SDLC and software supply chain (SLSA, SBOM, Sigstore), secrets, cryptography and post-quantum readiness, detection and response, NIST CSF 2.0 and security for event and data platforms.
t: Security Architecture: Zero Trust, AppSec, Supply Chain and Cryptography

b: Simple definition# AI security protects systems built on machine learning, especially large language models (LLMs) and AI agents, from manipulation, data leakage, misuse and failure. It also protects people and organisations from harm caused by those systems. The problem# LLMs mix instructions and data in the same channel (text). Any text the model reads, whether a user prompt, an email, a web page, a PDF or a tool result, can try to change its behaviour. When the model can also act by calling tools, moving money, sending emails or running code, a manipulated model becomes a manipulated employee with system access. Threat landscape# OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025)# # Risk One-line example LLM01 Prompt Injection A hidden instruction in an uploaded document makes the assistant leak data LLM02 Sensitive Information Disclosure The model reveals other customers&rsquo; data or secrets LLM03 Supply Chain A poisoned model, dataset, plugin or package LLM04 Data and Model Poisoning Manipulated training or fine-tuning data plants a backdoor LLM05 Improper Output Handling Model output rendered as HTML or executed as SQL causes XSS or injection LLM06 Excessive Agency The agent has more tools, permissions or autonomy than needed LLM07 System Prompt Leakage Secrets or logic in system prompts get exposed LLM08 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses RAG returns documents the user may not see; embedding inversion LLM09 Misinformation Confident hallucinations drive wrong decisions LLM10 Unbounded Consumption Token floods, runaway agent loops, denial of wallet OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications (2026)# Published in December 2025 for agents that plan, use tools and act: ID Risk ASI01 Agent Goal Hijack: content the agent reads redirects its objective ASI02 Tool Misuse and Exploitation ASI03 Identity and Privilege Abuse: agents inheriting or escalating credentials ASI04 Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities: tools, MCP servers, agent registries ASI05 Unexpected Code Execution ASI06 Memory and Context Poisoning ASI07 Insecure Inter-Agent Communication ASI08 Cascading Failures ASI09 Human–Agent Trust Exploitation: users over-trusting or being manipulated ASI10 Rogue Agents: needs behavioural monitoring and kill switches MITRE ATLAS catalogues real adversarial tactics and techniques against AI systems, in ATT&amp;CK style, for red teaming and detection. Prompt injection: why it is hard# Direct injection: the user types &ldquo;ignore previous instructions…&rdquo;. Indirect injection: the attack is in content the model processes, such as an email, web page, PDF, code comment, calendar invite or tool output. The user may be the victim, not the attacker. There is no complete fix today. Models cannot reliably separate instructions from data. Classifiers and &ldquo;guardrail&rdquo; models reduce the risk but can be bypassed. Key conceptDesign as if injection will succeed Assume the model can be manipulated. Then limit what a manipulated model can reach (data) and do (tools). The security boundary must be outside the model: in authorisation, tool design, approvals and sandboxing. Design patterns that limit the blast radius: Pattern Idea Least agency Expose only the tools and permissions the task needs; read-only by default Human-in-the-loop Require approval for consequential actions (payments, emails, deletions) User-scoped credentials Tools act as the user (delegated OAuth), never with a god-mode service account Plan-then-execute / dual LLM A privileged planner never reads untrusted content; a quarantined model processes untrusted data and returns structured, validated values Action-selector The model picks from a fixed set of safe actions instead of generating free-form calls Taint tracking (CaMeL-style) Track which values came from untrusted sources and block them from flowing into sensitive tool parameters Output encoding and validation Treat model output as untrusted input: escape it, validate it against schemas, and never execute it directly Reference architecture: defence in depth# Defence in depth for an LLM application or agent · drawn with Archify · zoom, guided views, search and SVG/PNG export. Open full screen ↗ Layer Controls AI gateway Authentication, rate and token limits, input and output guardrails (injection and jailbreak classifiers, PII detection and redaction, topic filters), model routing, cost quotas Application / agent Hardened system prompts (no secrets in them), structured outputs, tool allow-lists, step and budget limits, loop detection Retrieval (RAG) Permission-aware retrieval (filter by the user&rsquo;s ACLs at query time), document classification, source attribution, content sanitisation Tools / MCP Least privilege, user-delegated OAuth, input validation, sandboxed execution, approval for risky actions, idempotency Authorisation A policy engine (OPA, Cedar) decides each tool call from user, agent, action, resource and context Model Vetted provider or model with a contract (no training on your data, data residency); or self-hosted with signed weights Observability Full traces of prompts, retrieved documents, tool calls and decisions (with PII handling); anomaly detection; evaluation results RAG and data leakage# Never put all documents in one shared index and rely on the prompt to &ldquo;only answer from allowed docs&rdquo;. Filter in the retriever using the requesting user&rsquo;s entitlements, and propagate document ACLs into vector metadata. Classify documents and exclude restricted classes from general assistants. Watch for embedding inversion and membership inference. Treat embeddings as sensitive as their sources. Sanitise retrieved content (strip hidden text and active content) and mark it as untrusted data in the prompt. Tool, MCP and agent security# MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers are code with access. Vet them like dependencies: pin versions and verify publishers run them in sandboxes restrict network egress use the protocol&rsquo;s OAuth-based authorisation for remote

b: Simple definition# Data security protects the confidentiality, integrity and availability of data against unauthorised access, change or loss. Privacy engineering makes sure personal data is collected and used only for legitimate, stated purposes, minimised, and handled according to people&rsquo;s rights. The problem# Data is copied into events, lakes, caches, logs, backups, test environments and now embeddings and prompts. Every copy is a breach waiting to happen. Regulators (GDPR, India&rsquo;s DPDP Act, PCI DSS, banking secrecy rules) impose heavy fines and reporting duties. The goal is to reduce where sensitive data lives and protect what remains with layered controls. Step 1: classify# Level Examples Typical controls Public Product brochures Integrity only Internal Org charts, internal docs Authentication Confidential Customer names, account balances, transactions Encryption, RBAC/ABAC, masking, logging Restricted Card numbers (PAN), authentication data, Aadhaar or national IDs, health data, keys Tokenisation, HSM, strict need-to-know, segregated environments Automate discovery and tagging (catalog classifiers, cloud DLP and data security posture management (DSPM) tools), and propagate tags through lineage. Step 2: protect data in each state# State Controls In transit TLS 1.3 everywhere; mTLS service to service; no plaintext Kafka, JDBC or internal HTTP At rest Disk, database and object-storage encryption with customer-managed keys where required In use Field- and application-level encryption, tokenisation, masking; confidential computing (TEEs) for highly sensitive processing Keys: envelope encryption# Envelope encryption with KMS / HSM flowchart LR APP[&#34;Application&#34;] --&gt;|&#34;1 generate data key&#34;| KMS[&#34;KMS / HSM&lt;br/&gt;master key never leaves&#34;] KMS --&gt;|&#34;2 plaintext DEK + DEK encrypted under KEK&#34;| APP APP --&gt;|&#34;3 encrypt data with DEK,&lt;br/&gt;discard plaintext DEK&#34;| STORE[&#34;Store ciphertext + encrypted DEK&#34;] STORE -.-&gt;|&#34;4 decrypt: send encrypted DEK to KMS&#34;| KMS Key encryption keys (KEKs) live in a KMS or HSM (FIPS 140-3). Data encryption keys (DEKs) encrypt the data. Rotate keys, separate duties (key admins are not data admins), log every key use, and consider BYOK or HYOK for regulated workloads. Plan crypto-agility for post-quantum migration. See security architecture. Tokenisation vs encryption vs masking# Technique What it does Reversible? Use for Encryption Ciphertext via key Yes, with the key Storage and transport; fields that are needed back Tokenisation Replaces the value with a random token; mapping in a secure vault (or vaultless format-preserving tokens) Only via the token service PAN (shrinks PCI scope), national IDs, account numbers in analytics Format-preserving encryption (FPE) Ciphertext keeps the format (16 digits stays 16 digits) Yes Legacy systems that validate formats Static masking Irreversibly replaces values in copies No Test and dev data Dynamic masking Masks at query time based on the user Underlying data unchanged Analysts see XXXX-1234; fraud team sees the full value Hashing (salted, keyed) One-way digest No Joins on identifiers without revealing them Key conceptTokenise early, de-tokenise rarely Tokenise sensitive identifiers at the edge of the platform (API gateway, ingestion). Most services and analytics then work with tokens, and only a few tightly controlled services can de-tokenise. That shrinks breach impact and audit scope. Access control: RBAC, ABAC and fine-grained security# RBAC: permissions by role (analyst, fraud-investigator). Simple, but suffers role explosion. ABAC / policy-based: decisions from attributes of the user (department, clearance, location), the data (classification, region, owner) and the context (purpose, time, device). It scales better. Row-level security: an analyst in India sees only Indian customers. Column-level security and masking: a PII column is masked unless the user has purpose fraud-investigation. Tag-based policies in the catalog (Unity Catalog, Polaris, Lake Formation, Snowflake, Immuta, Privacera) apply one rule to every table tagged pii. Policy as code: OPA/Rego or Cedar, reviewed and tested like software. Just-in-time, time-boxed access with approval for restricted data, plus regular access recertification. Data loss prevention and monitoring# DLP on egress paths: email, web uploads, endpoints, and GenAI prompts, where sensitive data pasted into external AI tools is a major leak vector. Database activity monitoring and query logs sent to the SIEM; alerts on unusual volumes, new access paths or bulk exports. DSPM continuously discovers sensitive data and risky exposure across cloud stores. Canary tokens in sensitive datasets detect exfiltration. Privacy by design# The GDPR principles (Article 5), mirrored by India&rsquo;s DPDP Act 2023: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency (DPDP: notice and consent, or legitimate uses) Purpose limitation: use data only for the stated purpose Data minimisation: collect only what is needed Accuracy Storage limitation: retention schedules, deletion Integrity and confidentiality Accountability: prove it Engineering patterns: Purpose-tagged data and purpose-based access (&ldquo;marketing&rdquo; cannot read data collected for &ldquo;fraud&rdquo;). Consent records as data, checked by services (consent management platforms; under DPDP, Consent Managers registered with the Data Protection Board). Data subject rights workflows: access, correction, erasure, portability, with lineage to find every copy. Pseudonymisation (replace identifiers; re-identification possible with a separately held key) is still personal data under GDPR. Anonymisation (irreversible, with no reasonable means to re-identify) is outside GDPR&rsquo;s scope, but true anonymisation is hard. DPIAs (data protection impact assessments) for high-risk processing. Privacy-enhancing technologies (PETs)# PET Use Differential privacy Publish statistics without

b: Simple definition# In an event-driven architecture (EDA), services announce facts that happened (&ldquo;PaymentAuthorised&rdquo;) instead of telling other services what to do. Interested services react to those events in their own time. The producer does not know, or need to know, who is listening. The problem# With synchronous REST chains, every service must be up for the request to succeed. Latencies add up, and adding a new consumer means changing the caller. A checkout that calls payments, then inventory, then loyalty, then email fails if email is slow. EDA decouples in time and in knowledge, so services can scale, fail and evolve independently. Messages: events, commands and queries# Type Meaning Naming Coupling Event A fact that happened; immutable Past tense: OrderPlaced Producer does not know the consumers Command A request for one specific receiver to do something; may be refused Imperative: ReserveStock Sender knows the receiver Query A request for data GetBalance Synchronous, usually A common split is domain events, which stay inside a bounded context, and integration events, which form the published, versioned contract for other teams. Do not leak internal domain events as public contracts. The four event patterns (Martin Fowler)# Four things people mean by event-driven flowchart TB EN[&#34;Event notification&lt;br/&gt;&#39;OrderPlaced id=42&#39; — consumer calls back for details&#34;] ECST[&#34;Event-carried state transfer&lt;br/&gt;event carries the data consumers need&#34;] ES[&#34;Event sourcing&lt;br/&gt;events ARE the system of record&#34;] CQRS[&#34;CQRS&lt;br/&gt;separate write and read models&#34;] Event notification: a thin event with an ID. It is simple, but consumers call back for the details, which reintroduces coupling and load. Event-carried state transfer (ECST): the event carries the data consumers need, so they keep a local copy and stay available when the producer is down. Data is duplicated and eventually consistent. Event sourcing: state is derived from an append-only sequence of events. See CQRS and event sourcing. CQRS: separate models for writes and reads, often fed by events. Choreography vs orchestration# Choreography Orchestration How Each service reacts to events and emits new ones A coordinator tells each service what to do Strengths Loose coupling, no central component Visible flow, easy to change, clear error handling Weaknesses The flow is implicit and spread across services, so it is hard to see and debug The orchestrator is a component you must make reliable Use when Few steps, simple reactions, broadcast facts Multi-step business processes with compensation, SLAs and audit Most real systems mix the two: orchestrate a business process (see sagas) and choreograph notifications around it. Designing events and topics# Event envelope. Use a consistent envelope, for example aligned with CloudEvents (a CNCF graduated specification): { &#34;specversion&#34;: &#34;1.0&#34;, &#34;id&#34;: &#34;8f3c2a8e-6d7b-4e39-9b58-2a1f0c3d9e11&#34;, &#34;source&#34;: &#34;payments-service&#34;, &#34;type&#34;: &#34;com.bank.payments.PaymentAuthorised.v1&#34;, &#34;time&#34;: &#34;2026-11-01T09:14:03.120Z&#34;, &#34;subject&#34;: &#34;payment/PAY-20261101-000042&#34;, &#34;datacontenttype&#34;: &#34;application/avro&#34;, &#34;data&#34;: { &#34;paymentId&#34;: &#34;PAY-20261101-000042&#34;, &#34;accountId&#34;: &#34;ACC-42&#34;, &#34;amount&#34;: &#34;125.00&#34;, &#34;currency&#34;: &#34;EUR&#34; } } Checklist: Unique event ID for de-duplication; event time as well as processing time. Key by the entity whose order matters (accountId, orderId). Topic naming: &lt;domain&gt;.&lt;entity&gt;.&lt;event&gt;.v&lt;major&gt;, for example payments.payment.authorised.v1. Alternatively use one topic per aggregate stream with typed events, if consumers need cross-event order for that entity. No secrets or unnecessary PII in events. Tokenise or reference sensitive data. Events are copied widely and retained. Correlation and causation IDs plus W3C traceparent headers, for tracing across services. Document with AsyncAPI (version 3.x) and register schemas. See Schemas and event contracts. Reliability building blocks# Problem Pattern &ldquo;I updated my DB but the event was lost&rdquo; Transactional outbox + CDC Duplicates from retries Idempotent consumer (processed-event table, natural keys, upserts) Events arrive out of order Key by entity; version numbers; ignore stale versions Poison events Retry topics plus a dead-letter topic Multi-step business process Saga with compensations Consumers need history Retention, compaction or an event store, plus replay Observability for asynchronous flows# Propagate trace context in headers. OpenTelemetry instrumentations for Kafka clients create producer and consumer spans linked across topics. Measure end-to-end latency (event time to processed time), consumer lag, DLT rates and retry rates per consumer group. Keep an event catalog: which services produce and consume which events and versions. Backstage, an EventCatalog or AsyncAPI docs can serve. When not to use EDA# When you need an immediate answer to the user (balance checks, validations): use a synchronous query. For simple CRUD with one consumer: a direct call is clearer. When the team cannot yet operate the platform, monitor lag or reason about eventual consistency. Common mistakes# Common mistakeCommands disguised as events &ldquo;SendEmailRequested&rdquo; consumed by exactly one service is a command. That is fine, but name and own it as one; it couples sender to receiver. Common mistakeEvent notification everywhere Thin events cause call-back storms to the producer. Carry the state consumers need (ECST) where availability matters. Common mistakePublishing your internal model Leaking database-shaped or internal domain events as public contracts freezes your internals. Publish deliberate, versioned integration events. Common mistakeChoreography for long business processes Ten services
