b: Simple definition# Transactional outbox: write the business change and the event to the same database in one transaction, then publish the event from the database to the broker. Change data capture (CDC): read a database&rsquo;s transaction log and stream every change as events. Idempotent consumer: a consumer that gives the same result whether a message arrives once or several times. Together they give effectively-once processing without distributed transactions. The problem# A service saves an order and then publishes OrderPlaced. If it crashes between the two, the order exists but no one hears about it. If it publishes first and the commit fails, everyone hears about an order that does not exist. Retries make it worse: brokers and networks deliver at least once, so duplicates will happen. The transactional outbox# Transactional outbox with change data capture · drawn with Archify · zoom, guided views, search and SVG/PNG export. Open full screen ↗ BEGIN; INSERT INTO orders (id, customer_id, total, status) VALUES (&#39;ORD-42&#39;, &#39;C-7&#39;, 125.00, &#39;PLACED&#39;); INSERT INTO outbox (id, aggregate_type, aggregate_id, type, payload, created_at) VALUES (&#39;8f3c…&#39;, &#39;order&#39;, &#39;ORD-42&#39;, &#39;OrderPlaced&#39;, &#39;{&#34;orderId&#34;:&#34;ORD-42&#34;,...}&#39;, now()); COMMIT; Both rows commit or neither does. A relay then publishes outbox rows to Kafka. Two ways to relay# Polling publisher Log-based CDC (Debezium) How A job selects unpublished rows, publishes them, then marks or deletes them Reads the DB log (PostgreSQL WAL, MySQL binlog, Oracle LogMiner or XStream, SQL Server CDC) Latency Poll interval Sub-second DB load Queries on the outbox table Minimal (reads the log) Ordering Careful with concurrent pollers Commit order preserved Ops Simple Run Kafka Connect + Debezium; manage replication slots Debezium (Debezium 3.x) has an Outbox Event Router transformation. It routes each outbox row to a topic based on aggregate_type, uses aggregate_id as the Kafka key and puts the payload in the record value. The outbox table can be cleaned immediately or by retention. TipSpring and Java options Spring Modulith&rsquo;s event publication registry persists application events transactionally and republishes incomplete ones, which is an outbox inside the application. For cross-service events at scale, Debezium CDC is the common choice. CDC beyond the outbox# CDC also streams every table change for replication, cache invalidation, search indexing and lakehouse ingestion. Raw table CDC exposes your internal schema as a contract, so prefer the outbox for integration events and raw CDC for data replication into platforms you own. Idempotent consumers# Delivery is at least once, so consumers must tolerate duplicates. Strategy How Good for Processed-message table (inbox) Insert event_id into a table with a unique key in the same transaction as the business change; skip on conflict General purpose Natural idempotency Upsert by business key; &ldquo;set status = SHIPPED&rdquo; not &ldquo;toggle&rdquo; State updates Version check Apply only if event.version &gt; current.version Out-of-order delivery too Conditional write UPDATE ... WHERE status = 'PENDING' State machines -- Inbox / processed-message table, same transaction as the business change INSERT INTO processed_events (consumer, event_id, processed_at) VALUES (&#39;ledger-posting&#39;, :eventId, now()) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING; -- 0 rows inserted = duplicate, so skip the business logic Keep processed IDs at least as long as the redelivery window (the topic retention or replay horizon). Idempotency keys for APIs# Clients also retry, after timeouts or double-clicks. For non-idempotent operations such as POST /payments: Idempotency-Key handling flowchart TB R[&#34;POST /payments&lt;br/&gt;Idempotency-Key: K&#34;] --&gt; Q{&#34;Key K seen?&#34;} Q --&gt;|&#34;no&#34;| S[&#34;store K + request hash, status IN_PROGRESS&#34;] --&gt; P[&#34;process&#34;] --&gt; SAVE[&#34;store response for K&#34;] --&gt; OK[&#34;return response&#34;] Q --&gt;|&#34;yes, completed, same hash&#34;| RET[&#34;return stored response&#34;] Q --&gt;|&#34;yes, in progress&#34;| CONF[&#34;409 / retry later&#34;] Q --&gt;|&#34;yes, different payload&#34;| ERR[&#34;422 key reuse error&#34;] The IETF Idempotency-Key HTTP header draft standardises this behaviour. Payment APIs such as Stripe and Adyen, and open-banking APIs, already use it. Ordering# Key events by aggregate ID, so all events for one order share a partition and stay in order. Include a per-aggregate sequence or version in each event. Consumers ignore stale or duplicate versions and can detect gaps. Do not depend on order across aggregates. Common mistakes# Common mistakePublishing to Kafka inside the DB transaction The broker is not part of the transaction. A rollback after the send leaves a phantom event. Use the outbox. Common mistakeIdempotency check in a separate transaction If the check commits but the business change fails, or the reverse, duplicates or losses return. Do both in one transaction. Common mistakeRaw table CDC as a public contract Consumers couple to your column names. Publish deliberate events through the outbox. Common mistakeForgetting replication-slot hygiene An abandoned Debezium slot makes PostgreSQL keep WAL forever and fill the disk. Monitor slot lag. Quick check# How does the outbox pattern solve the dual-write problem? The state change and the event are written in one local DB transaction. A separate relay publishes the event, so neither can exist without the other. Polling publisher vs CDC? Polling is simple but adds DB load and latency. CDC reads the transaction log with low latency and preserves commit order, but needs Debezium and Connect operations. What makes a consumer idempotent? Recording the processed event ID in the same transaction as the business change, or applying naturally idempotent, versioned updates. What should an API do when an Idempotency-Key is reused

b: The design brief# &ldquo;A bank operating in the EU and India wants one data platform for regulatory reporting, risk, fraud analytics, customer insights and GenAI. Today it has three warehouses, a Hadoop lake and hundreds of spreadsheet reports with conflicting numbers. Regulators have criticised its risk data aggregation.&rdquo; 1. Key decisions: Layer Choice Why Storage Object storage per region; Apache Iceberg tables Open, multi-engine, time travel for audit Catalog One Iceberg REST catalog (for example Polaris or Unity Catalog) per region, federated into an enterprise catalog (DataHub or Collibra) One policy plane; business glossary across regions Ingestion Debezium CDC + Kafka for core systems; Kafka Connect Iceberg sink; batch for files Low latency, low source load, replayable Processing Spark for batch, Flink for streaming, dbt for SQL transformations Right tool per workload Serving Trino or warehouse SQL for BI; Pinot or ClickHouse for real-time dashboards; feature store; vector index Fit to access pattern Orchestration Airflow 3 or Dagster with OpenLineage Lineage emitted automatically 3. EU personal data stays in the EU unless a transfer mechanism applies. Only metadata, lineage and aggregated or anonymised results cross borders. The same platform code is deployed to each region through GitOps, with policies as code. 4. Security design# Tokenise at ingestion: PAN, Aadhaar/PAN numbers, IBANs and phone numbers are tokenised by a regional token service (HSM-backed) before reaching bronze. Raw values live only in a restricted zone with separate accounts and keys. Classification tags are applied automatically (classifiers plus contracts) and inherited through lineage. ABAC policies in the catalog: classification, region, purpose and domain attributes. Column masks for PII; row filters by legal entity. Purpose-based access: requests state a purpose (fraud, risk, marketing) checked against consent and legal basis. Just-in-time access for restricted data, with approval and a time limit; quarterly recertification. Audit: every query logged to the SIEM; anomaly alerts for bulk exports. Keys: customer-managed keys per region and per zone; crypto-shredding for erasure in immutable stores. 5. Governance and quality# Data products per domain (Payments, Lending, Customer, Risk), each with an ODCS contract, an owner, SLOs and quality rules. Quality gates between layers. Critical failures block gold publication and alert the owner. Column-level lineage from source to regulatory report (BCBS 239), viewable by auditors. Reconciliation of gold risk data against finance ledgers daily, with breaks tracked to closure. 6. AI on the platform# Feature store built from gold products, with point-in-time correctness for training. RAG: documents are ingested into the catalog with classification. Embeddings are stored in a vector index with the source document ACLs. Retrieval filters by the requesting user&rsquo;s entitlements. Model governance: lineage from datasets to model to decisions. Credit-scoring models are treated as high-risk AI under the EU AI Act, with documentation, bias testing and human oversight. 7. Migration plan# Stand up the platform and catalog in one region; onboard 3 high-value domains (risk, payments, customer). Rebuild the top 20 regulatory reports on gold products with lineage; run old and new in parallel and reconcile. Decommission the warehouses domain by domain; migrate Hadoop tables to Iceberg (in-place metadata migration where possible). Roll out self-serve onboarding (templates, contracts, policies) to the remaining domains. 8. Trade-offs# Decision Benefit Cost Regional data planes Residency compliance Duplicate platform operations; cross-region analytics only on aggregates Tokenise at ingestion Most users never see raw PII; smaller audit scope Token service on the critical path; de-tokenisation workflows Open formats + one catalog No lock-in, one policy plane Integration effort across engines Data products with contracts Accountability, quality upstream Requires domain teams to staff data roles Quick check# How does the design satisfy RBI data localisation? Indian payment data is ingested and stored in an India-region data plane. Only metadata and aggregated or anonymised results leave the region. Where is PII tokenised and why? At ingestion, before bronze, so almost all downstream users and systems work with tokens. That reduces breach impact and audit scope. How is BCBS 239 addressed? Governed gold data products with quality gates, column-level lineage from source to report, owners, and daily reconciliation. How does RAG respect access rights? Embeddings carry the
d: A complete design for a bank's data and AI platform: requirements (BCBS 239, GDPR/DPDP, RBI localisation), lakehouse with Iceberg, ingestion via CDC and Kafka, medallion layers and data products, catalog-enforced security with tokenisation and ABAC, lineage and quality, regional data planes, AI and RAG access, and trade-offs.

b: Simple definition# FinTech regulations set legally binding requirements for how financial services protect money, data and customers, and how they stay operational. For architects, every regulation turns into non-functional requirements: security controls, data handling, resilience, auditability and reporting timelines. WarningNot legal advice This page summarises regulations as they affect system design, as of November 2026. Dates and details change. Confirm applicability and obligations with compliance and legal teams and the primary texts. The landscape at a glance# Regulations by concern flowchart TB subgraph CARD[&#34;Card data&#34;] PCI[&#34;PCI DSS v4.0.1&#34;] end subgraph RES[&#34;Operational resilience &amp; cyber&#34;] DORA[&#34;EU DORA&#34;] NIS2[&#34;EU NIS2&#34;] RBI[&#34;RBI cyber directions&#34;] SEBI[&#34;SEBI CSCRF&#34;] CERTIN[&#34;CERT-In directions&#34;] end subgraph PAY[&#34;Payments&#34;] PSD[&#34;PSD2 → PSD3 / PSR&#34;] IPR[&#34;EU Instant Payments Reg.&#34;] end subgraph DATA[&#34;Personal data&#34;] GDPR[&#34;EU GDPR&#34;] DPDP[&#34;India DPDP Act + Rules&#34;] end subgraph AI[&#34;AI &amp; products&#34;] AIA[&#34;EU AI Act&#34;] CRA[&#34;EU Cyber Resilience Act&#34;] end PCI DSS v4.0.1 (cards)# The Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard applies to anyone who stores, processes or transmits cardholder data. v4.0.1 (June 2024) is the only active version. Requirements that were &ldquo;future-dated&rdquo; became mandatory on 31 March 2025. The 12 requirements fall into six goals: secure network, protect account data, vulnerability management, strong access control, monitoring and testing, security policy. Architecturally important v4 requirements: 8.4.2: MFA for all access into the cardholder data environment (CDE). 6.4.3 and 11.6.1: inventory, authorise and integrity-check payment page scripts, and detect unauthorised changes. This counters Magecart-style skimming. 5.4.1: anti-phishing mechanisms. 3.5.1.1: keyed cryptographic hashes for PAN. 12.5.2: annual scope confirmation (every six months for service providers). The customised approach: meet a control objective in your own way, with a targeted risk analysis. Design lever: scope reduction. Tokenise PAN, use hosted payment fields or iframes and P2PE, and segment the network. Systems that see only tokens fall out of scope. PCI SSC ran a request for comments on the standard in mid-2026 to inform the next version, so watch for updates. DORA (EU Digital Operational Resilience Act)# Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 has applied since 17 January 2025 to banks, insurers, investment firms, payment and e-money institutions, crypto-asset service providers and their critical ICT providers. It is the lex specialis over NIS2 for the financial sector. Pillar What it requires architecturally ICT risk management An ICT risk framework; asset inventory; protection, detection, response and recovery; backup and restoration testing; segregation; change management Incident management and reporting Classify incidents; major ICT incidents: initial notification within 4 hours of classification (and within 24 hours of becoming aware), intermediate report within 72 hours, final report within one month Resilience testing Annual testing programme; threat-led penetration testing (TLPT) every 3 years for significant entities (TIBER-EU based; RTS adopted) ICT third-party risk Register of information for all ICT contracts; mandatory contract clauses; exit strategies; concentration risk Information sharing Voluntary threat intelligence sharing The ESAs designated the first critical ICT third-party providers (CTPPs), including major cloud and technology providers, in November 2025. They are now under direct EU oversight. Design implications: documented dependency maps, tested failover and restore, immutable logging for incident timelines, automated incident classification, and exit plans for cloud services (multi-cloud or portability where justified). NIS2 (Directive (EU) 2022/2555) applies to many other essential and important entities with similar requirements: risk measures, 24-hour early warning, 72-hour notification. Financial entities follow DORA instead. Payments: PSD2 → PSD3 / PSR, and instant payments# PSD2 (in force since 2018) introduced: Strong customer authentication (SCA): two of knowledge, possession, inherence, with dynamic linking (an authentication code tied to amount and payee) for remote payments. Exemptions exist for low value, trusted beneficiaries and transaction risk analysis. Open banking (access to accounts): banks must give licensed third parties (AISPs, PISPs) secure API access. This drove standards such as Berlin Group NextGenPSD2, UK Open Banking and FAPI security profiles. PSD3 and the Payment Services Regulation (PSR): political agreement was reached in November 2025, and final compromise texts were published in April 2026. Formal adoption is expected in late 2026, with application likely in 2027–2028. Expected changes: Fraud: liability shifts for certain impersonation scams (for example fraudsters posing as bank staff), fraud data sharing between providers, transaction monitoring requirements. SCA improvements: accessibility (not only smartphones), clearer rules for merchant-initiated transactions. Open banking: dedicated-interface performance rules and permission dashboards for customers. Payment and e-money institutions merge into one licensing regime. EU Instant Payments Regulation (2024/886): euro-area PSPs must send instant payments (from 9 October 2025), at the same price as standard transfers. Verification of Payee (IBAN–name check) has been required since October 2025. Sanctions screening is done daily against customer bases rather than per transaction. GDPR (EU personal data)# Principles: lawfulness, purpose limitation, minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, security, accountability. Data subject rights (access, rectification, erasure, portability, objection, rights on automated decisions under Article
d: What financial regulations mean for system design: PCI DSS v4.0.1, DORA and NIS2, PSD2 and PSD3/PSR with SCA and open banking, the Instant Payments Regulation, GDPR, the EU AI Act after the 2026 Digital Omnibus, the Cyber Resilience Act, UK and US rules, India's DPDP Act and Rules 2025, RBI and CERT-In directions, SEBI CSCRF, SWIFT CSP and BCBS 239, plus how to map controls once to many regulations.

b: Simple definition# A saga is a sequence of local transactions, one per service. If a step fails, the saga runs compensating transactions to semantically undo the steps that already succeeded. It replaces one big distributed transaction with steps that are each atomic, plus an explicit undo plan. The problem# Placing an order touches the order, payment, inventory and shipping services, each with its own database. 2PC is not an option (see distributed transactions). Without a pattern, a failure halfway through leaves money taken with no stock reserved, or stock held for an order that was never paid. Anatomy of a saga# Step type Meaning Example Compensatable Can be undone by a compensating transaction Reserve stock (release stock) Pivot The point of no return: after it, the saga must complete Capture payment, ship goods Retriable After the pivot; must eventually succeed, so retry until it does Send confirmation, update loyalty points Order your steps so that compensatable steps come first, then the pivot, then retriable steps. Key conceptCompensation is not rollback A compensation is a new business action (&ldquo;refund&rdquo;, &ldquo;release&rdquo;, &ldquo;cancel&rdquo;) that is visible and audited. It does not erase history. Some actions cannot be undone, such as an email that was sent; plan around them. Choreography# Each service listens for events and publishes its own. Choreographed order saga sequenceDiagram participant O as Order participant P as Payment participant I as Inventory O-&gt;&gt;P: OrderCreated (event) P-&gt;&gt;I: PaymentAuthorised (event) I--&gt;&gt;P: StockReservationFailed (event) P--&gt;&gt;O: PaymentVoided (event) O-&gt;&gt;O: mark order REJECTED Pros: no central coordinator; loose coupling; simple for 2–4 steps. Cons: the flow is implicit and spread across services, so it is hard to see the state of one order. Cyclic dependencies and &ldquo;who compensates what&rdquo; get messy as steps grow. Orchestration# An orchestrator owns the saga state and sends commands to each participant. Orchestrated saga with compensation · drawn with Archify · zoom, guided views, search and SVG/PNG export. Open full screen ↗ Pros: an explicit, testable flow; one place for timeouts, retries and compensation; easy to see &ldquo;where is order 42?&rdquo;; audit-friendly. Cons: the orchestrator is an extra component that must be durable and highly available, and logic can creep into it. Keep business rules in the participants. The saga as a state machine# Order saga state machine · drawn with Archify · zoom, guided views, search and SVG/PNG export. Open full screen ↗ Persist the saga state before each step. A crash then resumes from the last durable state instead of starting over or forgetting. Durable execution engines# Writing a reliable orchestrator yourself (state persistence, timers, retries, versioning) is hard. Durable execution platforms do it for you: Tool Model Temporal (and Cadence) Workflows as code (Java, Go, TypeScript, Python, .NET). Event-sourced history, automatic retries, timers, signals. Camunda 8 / Zeebe BPMN models; good when business analysts own the process AWS Step Functions, Azure Durable Functions, Google Workflows Managed state machines Restate, DBOS Lightweight durable execution embedded in services or the database Axon, Eventuate Tram Saga frameworks for event-driven Java // Temporal (Java): saga with compensation public class OrderWorkflowImpl implements OrderWorkflow { private final Activities act = Workflow.newActivityStub(Activities.class, ActivityOptions.newBuilder().setStartToCloseTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(30)) .setRetryOptions(RetryOptions.newBuilder().setMaximumAttempts(5).build()).build()); public OrderResult placeOrder(Order order) { Saga saga = new Saga(new Saga.Options.Builder().build()); try { act.createOrder(order); saga.addCompensation(act::rejectOrder, order.id()); act.authorisePayment(order); saga.addCompensation(act::voidPayment, order.id()); act.reserveStock(order); saga.addCompensation(act::releaseStock, order.id()); act.capturePayment(order); // pivot: no compensation after this point act.bookShipment(order); // retriable: retries until it succeeds return OrderResult.completed(order.id()); } catch (ActivityFailure e) { saga.compensate(); // runs compensations in reverse order return OrderResult.rejected(order.id(), e.getMessage()); } } } Isolation: the anomalies sagas allow# Sagas give up the &ldquo;I&rdquo; in ACID. Other transactions can see intermediate states: Anomaly Example Countermeasure Dirty read Another service reads an order that will be rejected Semantic lock: a PENDING status that readers respect Lost update A compensation overwrites a concurrent change Commutative updates (debit/credit, not &ldquo;set balance&rdquo;), versioning Non-repeatable read Price changes between steps Reread value, or pass the snapshot in the command Ordering Cancel arrives before create Handle empty compensation; idempotent, order-tolerant handlers Making sagas reliable# Every command and event goes through an outbox. Every participant is idempotent. Every step has a timeout. &ldquo;No answer&rdquo; is a state you handle. Compensations must be idempotent and retriable, and must eventually succeed. If they cannot, go to manual review with an alert. Put a saga ID and correlation ID on every message, and trace them with OpenTelemetry. Test failure at every step, including double delivery and out-of-order events. Durable execution frameworks offer replay and time-skipping tests. Common mistakes# Common mistakeNo compensation design until production Write the compensation for each step at design time. Ask &ldquo;how do we undo this?&rdquo; for every step. Common mistakePivot too early Capturing payment before stock is reserved forces refunds. Put compensatable steps first. Common mistakeChoreographing 10 steps No one can see the flow and failures get lost. Use an orchestrator for long processes. Common mistakeIgnoring isolation Other services read
d: Managing business transactions across services with sagas: local transactions and compensations, choreography vs orchestration, saga state machines, pivot and retriable steps, isolation countermeasures (semantic locks, commutative updates), durable execution with Temporal, and testing and observability.

b: Simple definition# An event contract is the agreed shape and meaning of an event: field names, types, required fields, semantics and service levels. A schema registry stores every version of that shape and checks that new versions do not break existing producers or consumers. The problem# Kafka stores bytes and does not check them. If a producer renames amount to value, every consumer breaks, and it may happen at 2 a.m., replaying data from last month. Contracts and compatibility checks turn that runtime outage into a failed build. Serialisation formats# Avro Protobuf JSON Schema Encoding Compact binary; schema needed to read Compact binary; field numbers Text JSON Evolution Excellent, with defaults Excellent, with field numbers Weaker and easy to get wrong Tooling Strong in data and Kafka ecosystems Strong in gRPC and polyglot services Human-readable, browser-friendly Typical use Kafka and data platforms Service-to-service and event mix Edge, low-volume, external partners Any of the three works with a registry. Pick one default per organisation. How a registry works# Schema registry on the write and read paths sequenceDiagram participant P as Producer participant R as Schema Registry participant K as Kafka participant C as Consumer P-&gt;&gt;R: register or lookup schema (subject payments-value) R--&gt;&gt;P: schema ID 17 (or reject if incompatible) P-&gt;&gt;K: [magic byte][schema ID 17][binary payload] C-&gt;&gt;K: fetch record C-&gt;&gt;R: get schema 17 (cached) C-&gt;&gt;C: deserialize with writer schema 17 + reader schema Each message carries only a small schema ID. Consumers fetch and cache the writer&rsquo;s schema and resolve it against their own reader schema. Registries include Confluent Schema Registry, Apicurio Registry (open source, by Red Hat), AWS Glue Schema Registry and Azure Schema Registry. Compatibility modes# Mode Guarantee Allowed change (Avro) Upgrade order BACKWARD (default) New consumers can read data written with the previous schema Delete fields; add optional fields with defaults Consumers first FORWARD Old consumers can read data written with the new schema Add fields; delete optional fields Producers first FULL Both directions Add or delete optional fields with defaults Any order *_TRANSITIVE The guarantee holds against all previous versions, not just the last Same, but stricter For long retention and replay TipUse transitive modes when you replay If consumers may replay months of history, the new reader must handle every old version. Use BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE or FULL_TRANSITIVE. Safe and breaking changes# Change Safe? Add an optional field with a default ✅ Remove an optional field ✅ (under backward compatibility) Rename a field ❌ Add the new field, deprecate the old one, remove it later (Avro aliases can help) Change a type (int → string) ❌ (only certain widenings such as int → long are allowed) Change meaning (cents → euros) ❌ and invisible to tools; always a new version Reuse a Protobuf field number ❌ Never; mark removed numbers as reserved For a breaking change, publish a new major version topic (...v2), run v1 and v2 in parallel while consumers migrate, then retire v1. Data contracts# A data contract goes beyond the schema. It is a versioned agreement between a producer and its consumers that covers: schema (structure and types) semantics (definitions, units, allowed values, PII classification) quality rules (not null, ranges, uniqueness, freshness) SLOs (latency, availability) ownership and support policies (retention, access, masking). Specifications such as the Open Data Contract Standard (ODCS, Bitol project, Linux Foundation) describe contracts in YAML. Some registries attach rules to schemas, for example data-quality conditions or field-level encryption tags enforced in the serialiser. # Simplified data contract (ODCS-style) apiVersion: v3.0.0 kind: DataContract id: payments-authorised version: 1.2.0 status: active owner: team-payments schema: - name: PaymentAuthorised properties: - { name: paymentId, logicalType: string, required: true, unique: true } - { name: accountId, logicalType: string, required: true, classification: confidential } - { name: amount, logicalType: number, required: true, quality: [{ rule: &#34;amount &gt; 0&#34; }] } - { name: currency, logicalType: string, required: true, examples: [&#34;EUR&#34;, &#34;INR&#34;] } slaProperties: - { property: latency, value: 5, unit: s } Governance in the delivery pipeline# Contracts checked before deploy flowchart LR PR[&#34;PR changes schema&#34;] --&gt; CI[&#34;CI: compatibility check&lt;br/&gt;against registry&#34;] --&gt; LINT[&#34;Lint: naming, docs,&lt;br/&gt;PII tags&#34;] --&gt; REV[&#34;Owner + consumer review&#34;] --&gt; REG[&#34;Register on deploy&#34;] CI --&gt;|&#34;incompatible&#34;| FAIL[&#34;Build fails&#34;] Store schemas in Git next to the producer code, and generate classes from them. Run compatibility checks in CI with the registry&rsquo;s Maven or Gradle plugins or its REST API. Turn off auto-registration in production producers, so only CI registers schemas. Publish AsyncAPI documents so consumers can discover topics, schemas and owners. Common mistakes# Common mistakeSchemaless JSON on shared topics Without a registry, the first breaking change is found in production by a consumer. Register schemas and enforce compatibility. Common mistakeCompatibility &ldquo;NONE&rdquo; to unblock a release Turning checks off moves the failure to runtime. Use a new versioned topic for breaking changes. Common mistakeChanging semantics without changing the schema Switching an amount from minor to major units passes every tool and corrupts every consumer. Version the meaning, not just the shape. Quick check# What does BACKWARD compatibility guarantee? Consumers using the new schema can read data written with the previous schema, so you upgrade consumers first. Why use a transitive compatibility mode? It checks the new schema against all earlier versions, which matters when consumers
d: Treating events as contracts: Avro vs Protobuf vs JSON Schema, schema registries, compatibility modes (backward, forward, full, transitive), safe and breaking changes, versioning strategies, data contracts, and governance in CI.

b: The design brief# &ldquo;A digital bank operating in the EU and India is launching card and account-to-account payments, an open-banking API for partners, and a GenAI assistant that answers customer questions and can initiate small transfers. Design the security architecture so that it is PCI DSS, DORA, PSD2/PSD3, GDPR/DPDP and RBI compliant, and can withstand a determined attacker.&rdquo; 1. Architecture overview# Secure, regulated real-time payments platform · drawn with Archify · zoom, guided views, search and SVG/PNG export. Open full screen ↗ 2. Threat model highlights (STRIDE on the key flows)# Flow / element Top threats Key mitigations Customer → edge Account takeover (S), bots and DDoS (D) Passkeys / FIDO2 + SCA, device binding, bot management, WAF, rate limits Partner → open-banking API Stolen tokens (S), BOLA (I) FAPI 2.0 (PAR, sender-constrained tokens via mTLS or DPoP), consent checks per object Payment service Tampered amount or payee (T), double spend (T) Signed requests, dynamic linking (SCA), idempotency keys, ledger invariants Card data PAN theft (I) Tokenise at the edge with hosted fields; vault and HSM in a minimal CDE Kafka events Eavesdropping or injection (I, T), rogue producer (S) mTLS, ACLs per principal, schema validation, no PAN or PII in events AI assistant Prompt injection leading to unauthorised transfer (E), data leakage (I) Least agency, user-scoped tools, step-up SCA for any payment, permission-aware RAG Admin and ops access Insider misuse (E, R) JIT privileged access, session recording, four-eyes approval, PAM Supply chain Malicious dependency or image (T) SBOM, SLSA provenance, cosign signatures, admission policies 3. Shrinking PCI scope# Card data never touches most systems flowchart LR APP[&#34;Mobile / web&lt;br/&gt;hosted card fields (iframe/SDK)&#34;] --&gt;|&#34;PAN over TLS&#34;| TOK[&#34;Tokenisation service&lt;br/&gt;+ HSM (CDE)&#34;] TOK --&gt;|&#34;token&#34;| APP APP --&gt;|&#34;token only&#34;| PAY[&#34;Payment service&lt;br/&gt;(out of CDE scope)&#34;] PAY --&gt;|&#34;token&#34;| TOK TOK --&gt;|&#34;PAN (detokenised)&#34;| NET[&#34;Card network / acquirer&#34;] The CDE contains only the tokenisation service, the HSM and the network connector, in a separate account or VPC with its own keys, its own admins and strict egress. Everything else (payment service, Kafka, lakehouse, analytics, AI) sees tokens. That moves them out of scope or reduces their scope, and limits breach impact. Payment page scripts are inventoried and integrity-monitored (PCI 6.4.3 and 11.6.1). MFA covers all CDE access (8.4.2). 4. Identity and zero trust# Customers: passkeys with risk-based step-up. SCA with dynamic linking for payments (PSD2). Device binding for UPI-style flows (NPCI/RBI). Staff: SSO with phishing-resistant MFA, ZTNA instead of VPN, and JIT privileged access with approval and recording. Workloads: SPIFFE/SPIRE or cloud workload identity, mesh mTLS, and authorisation policies per service. No static secrets; Vault issues dynamic database credentials. Partners: FAPI 2.0 and an mTLS certificate per partner, with consent records checked on every call. 5. Data protection# Envelope encryption with customer-managed keys in an HSM, separate per region and zone, and key-usage logs sent to the SIEM. Kafka: TLS, OAUTHBEARER, ACLs, field-level encryption for sensitive fields, and a 30-day retention cap on events containing personal data. Residency: Indian payment data stays in the India region (RBI). EU personal data stays in the EU, with only aggregates crossing. See the regulated data platform. Erasure: crypto-shredding for immutable logs and events. Retention schedules apply per data class. 6. The AI assistant, safely# Control Implementation Least agency Tools: getBalance, listTransactions, initiateTransfer(max ₹10,000 / €100). No admin tools. User-scoped access Tools call APIs with the customer&rsquo;s delegated token, never a service account Step-up for actions initiateTransfer creates a pending payment that the customer must approve with SCA in the app. The model cannot complete it. Permission-aware RAG Only public help content and the customer&rsquo;s own documents are retrievable Guardrails AI gateway: injection and PII classifiers, output schema validation, token and cost limits Transparency Discloses AI interaction (EU AI Act Article 50); a human handover path Evaluation Red-teamed before launch (injection, social engineering, data leakage), regression evaluations on each change See AI security. 7. Detection, response and reporting# Centralised, tamper-evident logs (retained for at least 1 year, with 180 days in India for CERT-In) feed the SIEM, SOAR playbooks and a 24×7 SOC. Detections are mapped to MITRE ATT&amp;CK. Automated incident classification against DORA criteria (clients affected, duration, geographic spread, data loss, critical services, economic impact). The SOC has pre-approved notification templates. Reporting clocks are wired into the runbooks: Regulator Clock DORA (EU) Initial notification within 4 h of classification (and 24 h of awareness); intermediate within 72 h; final within 1 month RBI Within 6 h, through RBI&rsquo;s reporting platform CERT-In Within 6 h GDPR / DPDP 72 h to the supervisory authority (GDPR); to the Data Protection Board and individuals (DPDP) 8. Resilience and third parties# Multi-AZ by default; tested regional failover for tier-0 services. Restore tests of the ledger and token vault each quarter. An annual DORA testing programme (vulnerability scans, scenario tests, chaos experiments) and TLPT every three years if designated. Register of information for all ICT providers (cloud, HSM-as-a-service, KYC, model API). Contractual clauses for audit and exit, and documented exit plans. The model provider is treated as a critical dependency, with a fallback model. 9. Compliance map (excerpt)# Requirement Satisfied by PCI DSS 3 &amp; 4 (protect PAN) Tokenisation, HSM, TLS 1.3, minimal CDE PCI DSS 8.4.2 (MFA into CDE)
d: An end-to-end security architecture for a cloud-native payments platform: threat model, PCI scope reduction with tokenisation and HSMs, zero trust and FAPI APIs, Kafka and data security, fraud and an AI assistant with guardrails, detection and DORA/RBI incident reporting, resilience testing, third-party risk, and the compliance map.

b: Simple definition# CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation): use one model to change data (commands) and one or more different models to read it (queries). Event sourcing: store every change as an immutable event, and derive current state by replaying them, instead of storing only the latest state. They are often used together, but each works without the other. The problem# One model serving both writes and reads is a compromise. Writes need invariants and validation; reads need denormalised, fast, query-specific views such as search, dashboards and statements. Separately, many domains (ledgers, claims, trading) need the full history: what happened, when and why. A table that holds only &ldquo;current balance&rdquo; cannot answer that. CQRS# CQRS with event-driven read models · drawn with Archify · zoom, guided views, search and SVG/PNG export. Open full screen ↗ Command side: handles intent (TransferMoney), loads the aggregate, enforces rules and stores the change. Events flow (through the outbox or the event store) to projectors. Read side: one read model per need, such as Elasticsearch or OpenSearch for search, Redis for hot lookups, a columnar store for analytics, or a SQL view for statements. Levels of CQRS: Separate command and query classes on the same database (cheap and common). Separate read tables updated in the same transaction. Separate read stores updated asynchronously from events. This is eventually consistent. Event sourcing# State is a left fold over events flowchart LR E1[&#34;AccountOpened&lt;br/&gt;v1&#34;] --&gt; E2[&#34;MoneyDeposited 100&lt;br/&gt;v2&#34;] --&gt; E3[&#34;MoneyWithdrawn 30&lt;br/&gt;v3&#34;] --&gt; E4[&#34;MoneyDeposited 50&lt;br/&gt;v4&#34;] E4 --&gt; S[&#34;Current state&lt;br/&gt;balance = 120, version 4&#34;] How a command works: Load the aggregate&rsquo;s events (or the latest snapshot plus later events) and rebuild its state. Validate the command against that state. Append new events with optimistic concurrency (&ldquo;expected version = 4&rdquo;). On conflict, reload and retry. Publish the events to projections and other services. // Aggregate (simplified) class Account { private BigDecimal balance = BigDecimal.ZERO; private long version; List&lt;Event&gt; handle(Withdraw cmd) { if (balance.compareTo(cmd.amount()) &lt; 0) throw new InsufficientFunds(); return List.of(new MoneyWithdrawn(cmd.accountId(), cmd.amount())); } void apply(MoneyDeposited e) { balance = balance.add(e.amount()); version++; } void apply(MoneyWithdrawn e) { balance = balance.subtract(e.amount()); version++; } } Benefits# A complete audit trail by construction, which regulators love. Temporal queries: &ldquo;what was the balance on 31 March?&rdquo; Rebuild or create read models by replaying events, including new ones you had not imagined. A natural fit with event-driven integration. Costs and hard parts# Challenge Approach Long event streams Snapshots every N events Changing event schemas Upcasting (transform old events on read), versioned events, never edit history Querying Always through projections; the event store is not for ad-hoc queries Eventual consistency of reads Read-your-writes via version tokens, or query the write side for critical checks GDPR / DPDP erasure Crypto-shredding: encrypt personal data per subject and delete the key; or keep PII outside events Team learning curve Start with one bounded context where history matters Read-model consistency# After a command, the read model may lag by milliseconds to seconds. Options: Return the new version from the command; the UI polls or waits until the read model reaches that version. Optimistic UI: show the expected result immediately. For critical decisions, read from the write model, never from a projection. Tools# Tool Notes KurrentDB (formerly EventStoreDB) Purpose-built event store with streams and subscriptions Axon Framework / Axon Server Java CQRS + event sourcing + sagas Marten (.NET, on PostgreSQL), Eventuous Event sourcing on familiar databases PostgreSQL event table events(stream_id, version, type, data, metadata) with a unique (stream_id, version) Kafka Great for distributing events; poor as the only event store for aggregate loading (no efficient per-entity reads or optimistic concurrency) When to use (and not)# Use CQRS when… Use event sourcing when… Avoid when… Read and write loads or shapes differ greatly Audit history is a core requirement (ledgers, claims, trading) Simple CRUD Many specialised views of the same data You need temporal queries and replays The team is new to DDD and events, and the domain is not complex You need to scale reads independently The domain is naturally event-based Strong consistency is needed everywhere on reads Common mistakes# Common mistakeEvent sourcing the whole system Apply it to the bounded contexts where history matters. Use plain CRUD elsewhere. Common mistakeUsing Kafka as the event store for aggregates Loading one aggregate means scanning a partition, and there is no expected-version check. Use an event store or DB table and publish to Kafka. Common mistakePersonal data in immutable events Erasure becomes impossible. Use crypto-shredding or references. Common mistakeValidating commands against read models Projections are stale, so decisions can violate invariants. Validate against the aggregate. Quick check# What does CQRS separate? The model that handles commands (writes, with invariants) from the models that serve queries (reads, denormalised per use). How is state derived in event sourcing? By replaying the aggregate&rsquo;s events in order, optionally starting from a snapshot. How do you handle a changed event schema? Version events and upcast old versions when reading. Never modify stored history. How can event-sourced systems meet GDPR erasure? Crypto-shredding: encrypt personal fields per data subject and delete the key, or keep PII out of events. b: Simple definition# Stream processing computes results continuously as events arrive: filtering, enriching, aggregating, joining and detecting patterns. Batch processing instead waits for a complete dataset. The result is another stream, a table or an action, available in milliseconds to seconds. The problem# Fraud must be stopped before money leaves. Risk limits, customer notifications and dashboards lose value with every minute of delay. Running batch jobs more often does not scale and cannot handle late or out-of-order events correctly. Core concepts# Concept Meaning Stateless operation Each event is handled alone: map, filter, route, mask Stateful operation Needs memory of earlier events: counts, sums, joins, deduplication, pattern detection Event time When the event happened (in the payload) Processing time When the processor sees it Watermark The processor&rsquo;s estimate that &ldquo;no more events older than T will arrive&rdquo;. It lets windows close. Window A finite slice of an infinite stream State backend Where keyed state lives: memory, RocksDB, or remote / disaggregated storage Checkpoint A consistent snapshot of all state and source offsets, used for recovery Event time and watermarks# Mobile payments may arrive minutes late, and partitions progress at different speeds. Processing by event time gives correct results regardless of arrival order. Watermarks trade completeness against latency: Watermark with 5 seconds bounded out-of-orderness flowchart LR E1[&#34;event t=10:00:02&#34;] --&gt; W[&#34;watermark = max event time − 5s&#34;] E2[&#34;event t=10:00:09&#34;] --&gt; W E3[&#34;late event t=10:00:01&lt;br/&gt;arrives after window closed&#34;] --&gt; L[&#34;allowed lateness → update&lt;br/&gt;or side output for late data&#34;] W --&gt; C[&#34;window [10:00:00, 10:00:05) closes&lt;br/&gt;when watermark ≥ 10:00:05&#34;] Set the out-of-orderness bound from measured lateness (for example p99). Use idleness detection, so one quiet partition does not stall the watermark. Route late events to a side output rather than silently dropping them. Windows# Window Shape Example Tumbling Fixed size, no overlap Payments per merchant per minute Hopping / sliding Fixed size, overlapping Spend over the last 1 hour, updated every 5 minutes Session Activity separated by a gap A user&rsquo;s banking session Global + trigger Custom Every 100 events Joins# Stream–stream join (windowed): match PaymentInitiated with PaymentConfirmed within 10 minutes. Stream–table join: enrich each payment with the latest customer risk profile from a compacted topic or CDC stream (a temporal or lookup join). Interval join: events from two streams within a time bound of each other. State, checkpoints and exactly-once# Flink checkpoint barrier flowchart LR SRC[&#34;Kafka source&lt;br/&gt;offsets&#34;] --&gt;|&#34;barrier n&#34;| OP1[&#34;keyBy(account)&lt;br/&gt;window state&#34;] --&gt;|&#34;barrier n&#34;| SINK[&#34;Kafka sink&lt;br/&gt;transaction&#34;] OP1 -.-&gt;|&#34;snapshot state n&#34;| STORE[&#34;Durable checkpoint storage&lt;br/&gt;(S3, HDFS)&#34;] SRC -.-&gt;|&#34;offsets n&#34;| STORE SINK -.-&gt;|&#34;pre-commit txn n&#34;| STORE Flink injects barriers into the stream. Every operator snapshots its state when the barrier passes. The Kafka sink pre-commits a transaction and commits it only when the checkpoint completes (two-phase commit), giving end-to-end exactly-once from Kafka to Kafka. After a failure, Flink restores the last checkpoint and rewinds the source offsets. Apache Flink vs Kafka Streams# Apache Flink Kafka Streams Form Distributed processing engine (cluster, Kubernetes operator) Java library inside your application Sources and sinks Kafka, files, CDC, JDBC, Iceberg, Pulsar, Kinesis and many more Kafka in, Kafka out State RocksDB or disaggregated state (Flink 2.x ForSt on object storage) RocksDB plus changelog topics APIs DataStream, Table API, Flink SQL, CEP, PyFlink Streams DSL, Processor API Scale Very large, multi-tenant Scales with your app instances and partitions Best for Complex pipelines, large state, SQL analytics, many systems Kafka-centric microservices doing joins and aggregations What is new: Flink 2.0 (2025) introduced disaggregated state management (state on remote storage with a local cache), a materialised-table model that unifies batch and streaming, and removed old APIs such as DataSet and the Scala API. Flink 2.2 (December 2025) focused on real-time AI: ML_PREDICT model inference in Flink SQL and a VECTOR_SEARCH function for streaming similarity search, plus scheduling improvements. Kafka Streams gained server-side rebalancing (KIP-1071, GA with a limited feature set in Kafka 4.2). Flink SQL example: velocity check# -- Payments per card in 10-minute hopping windows; flag bursts CREATE TABLE payments ( payment_id STRING, card_token STRING, merchant_id STRING, amount DECIMAL(18,2), country STRING, event_time TIMESTAMP(3), WATERMARK FOR event_time AS event_time - INTERVAL &#39;5&#39; SECOND ) WITH (&#39;connector&#39; = &#39;kafka&#39;, &#39;topic&#39; = &#39;payments.authorised.v1&#39;, &#39;format&#39; = &#39;avro-confluent&#39;, ...); INSERT INTO fraud_alerts SELECT card_token, window_start, window_end, COUNT(*) AS txn_count, SUM(amount) AS total, COUNT(DISTINCT country) AS countries FROM TABLE(HOP(TABLE payments, DESCRIPTOR(event_time), INTERVAL &#39;1&#39; MINUTE, INTERVAL &#39;10&#39; MINUTE)) GROUP BY card_token, window_start, window_end HAVING COUNT(*) &gt; 8 OR COUNT(DISTINCT country) &gt; 2; A real-time fraud scoring pipeline# Real-time fraud scoring with Kafka and Flink · drawn with Archify · zoom, guided views, search and SVG/PNG export. Open full screen ↗ Payment and device events land on Kafka topics keyed by account or card token. A Flink job computes features in event-time windows (velocity, spend, new device, geo distance), keeping keyed state with checkpoints. Features are written to a low-latency feature cache, which the authorisation service reads

b: The design brief# &ldquo;Customers buy products online. An order must reserve stock, take payment and book delivery. Customers track their order in real time. Peak is 2,000 orders per second during sales. We must never charge for an order we cannot fulfil, and never ship an unpaid order.&rdquo; 1. Bounded contexts and data ownership# Service Owns Database Order Order lifecycle PostgreSQL Payment Authorisations, captures, refunds PostgreSQL (PCI-scoped) Inventory Stock levels, reservations PostgreSQL with row locks per SKU Shipping Shipments, carrier bookings PostgreSQL Order tracking (read) Denormalised order view OpenSearch + Redis Each service owns its data, and no service reads another&rsquo;s database. 2. The orchestrated saga# The Order Saga runs on Temporal. Steps are ordered so that compensatable steps come first, then the pivot, then retriable steps: # Step Type Compensation 1 Create order PENDING Compensatable Mark REJECTED 2 Authorise payment (hold) Compensatable Void the authorisation 3 Reserve stock (with 15-min expiry) Compensatable Release the reservation 4 Capture payment Pivot (refund only by a separate business process) 5 Book shipment Retriable none; retry, with ops escalation 6 Confirm order, notify Retriable none See the saga sequence and state machine. 3. Messaging and reliability# The Temporal worker calls each service&rsquo;s API with an idempotency key of sagaId + step. Services publish domain events (OrderConfirmed, StockReserved) through outbox + Debezium to Kafka for read models, analytics and notifications. Consumers are idempotent (inbox table) and keyed by orderId. Stock reservations expire automatically, so a stuck saga cannot hold stock forever. 4. CQRS for order tracking# Order tracking read model flowchart LR OE[&#34;Order events&#34;] --&gt; PR[&#34;Tracking projector&#34;] PE[&#34;Payment events&#34;] --&gt; PR SE[&#34;Shipping events&#34;] --&gt; PR PR --&gt; OS[&#34;OpenSearch: search orders&#34;] PR --&gt; RD[&#34;Redis: order status by ID&#34;] UI[&#34;Customer app&#34;] --&gt; API[&#34;Tracking API&#34;] --&gt; RD The customer sees status within about 1 second of each step. The API returns the version so the UI can wait for read-your-writes after placing an order. The projector is rebuildable from Kafka history (30-day retention plus the lakehouse for older events). 5. Failure scenarios# Scenario Behaviour Inventory says &ldquo;out of stock&rdquo; Compensate: void the authorisation, reject the order, notify &ldquo;sorry, no charge&rdquo; Payment service times out on authorise Temporal retries with the same idempotency key. After N tries, query the status; if unknown, compensate safely (void is idempotent and handles &ldquo;no auth found&rdquo;). Orchestrator worker crashes mid-saga Temporal replays the workflow history and resumes at the next step Capture succeeds, shipping fails Past the pivot: retry with backoff; after the SLA, escalate to ops (manual booking) Duplicate PlaceOrder click API idempotency key returns the original order Kafka consumer replays events Inbox de-duplication; versioned updates ignore stale events Stock reservation expires before capture Capture step re-validates the reservation; if lost, compensate the earlier steps 6. Consistency guarantees (state them explicitly)# Strong within each service (ACID); stock per SKU uses row locks or conditional updates (available &gt;= qty). Eventual across services. The saga guarantees the business invariants: no capture without a reservation, and no shipment without a capture. Eventual for tracking views (about 1 s). Daily reconciliation: payments against orders against shipments. Breaks are investigated. 7. Scale# 2,000 orders/s × about 6 steps gives about 12,000 activity executions per second. Use a Temporal cluster (or Temporal Cloud) sized with sufficient history shards, and partition task queues by service. Hot SKUs (flash sales): pre-split stock into buckets or use a reservation token pool to avoid single-row lock contention. 8. Observability# Saga ID = correlation ID across Temporal, HTTP headers and Kafka headers, with OpenTelemetry traces. Dashboards: sagas by state, compensation rate, step latency, stuck sagas older than their SLA, DLT counts. Alerts: compensation failures (manual review queue), reconciliation breaks. 9. Trade-offs# Choice Why Cost Orchestration (Temporal) Visible, testable, durable flow Platform to run, or a managed service Authorise then capture Avoids refunds for most failures Authorisations expire; capture must happen within days Reservation expiry Self-healing Edge cases when the saga is slower than the expiry CQRS tracking Fast, scalable reads Eventual consistency, projector to operate Quick check# Why authorise before reserving stock, and capture only after? Authorisation is compensatable (void), while capture is the pivot. Charging only after stock is secured avoids refunds. What prevents stock being held forever by a stuck saga? Reservations carry an expiry. Separately, the saga has timeouts that trigger compensation. How does the customer see their order immediately after placing it? The API returns a version, and the UI waits for the read model to reach it (read-your-writes), or shows an optimistic status. What invariant does the saga guarantee across services? No capture without a stock reservation, and no shipment without a capture. Summary# Clear data ownership, an orchestrated saga with ordered steps, and expiring reservations. Outbox, idempotency and inbox make messaging reliable; CQRS gives real-time tracking. State the consistency guarantees explicitly, and back them with reconciliation. References# Chris Richardson, Microservices Patterns (Manning), chapters on sagas and CQRS. Temporal, Saga pattern and samples.
d: A complete design for e-commerce or banking-product order processing across microservices: service boundaries, the orchestrated saga with Temporal, outbox and CDC, idempotency, CQRS read models for order tracking, failure scenarios, consistency guarantees, observability and trade-offs.

b: The design brief# &ldquo;Design the core of a bank&rsquo;s instant payments service. Customers send money from mobile and web; payments must settle in under 10 seconds, end to end, 24×7. Each payment must be fraud-checked, posted to the ledger exactly once, notified to both parties and reconciled with the scheme daily.&rdquo; 1. Requirements# Type Requirement Functional Initiate, validate, fraud-check, reserve funds, submit to the scheme (for example SEPA Instant, UPI or FedNow), confirm, post to the ledger, notify, reconcile Throughput 3,000 payments/s average, 15,000/s peak (salary days, festivals) Latency Under 10 s end to end (scheme rule); the internal path, excluding the scheme, at p99 under 1.5 s Correctness No double debit, no lost payment; every state change auditable Availability 99.99%; survive the loss of an AZ with no data loss, and a region with RPO ≈ 0 for the ledger Compliance PSD2/PSD3 SCA, PCI DSS (for card-funded flows), DORA, RBI/NPCI rules (for UPI), GDPR/DPDP 2. The key decision: what is synchronous?# The customer is waiting, so the critical path is synchronous and as short as possible. Everything else is asynchronous through events. Synchronous critical path vs asynchronous side effects flowchart LR subgraph SYNC[&#34;Synchronous: customer waits&#34;] A[&#34;API gateway&lt;br/&gt;SCA, idempotency key&#34;] --&gt; P[&#34;Payment service&lt;br/&gt;validate, state machine&#34;] P --&gt; F[&#34;Fraud score lookup&lt;br/&gt;under 50 ms&#34;] P --&gt; L[&#34;Ledger: reserve funds&#34;] P --&gt; S[&#34;Scheme gateway&lt;br/&gt;submit + confirm&#34;] end subgraph ASYNC[&#34;Asynchronous: events on Kafka&#34;] E[&#34;payment events&#34;] --&gt; N[&#34;Notifications&#34;] E --&gt; R[&#34;Reconciliation&#34;] E --&gt; AN[&#34;Analytics / lakehouse&#34;] E --&gt; FS[&#34;Fraud features update&#34;] end P --&gt;|&#34;outbox&#34;| E 3. Topics and keys# Topic Key Retention Notes payments.payment.lifecycle.v1 paymentId 30 days + tiered All state changes for one payment, in order payments.account.activity.v1 accountId 30 days For per-account ordering (balance views, limits) fraud.features.v1 cardOrAccountToken compacted Latest features per entity notifications.requests.v1 customerId 7 days Consumed by a share group (queue semantics) *.dlt same 30 days Dead letters, alerted RF=3, min.insync.replicas=2, rack-aware across 3 AZs. Size partitions for peak: 15,000/s at roughly 1–2 MB/s each needs well over 48 partitions for consumer parallelism, so plan 96–192 with growth. Use Avro with FULL_TRANSITIVE compatibility, and no PII beyond tokens in events. 4. Correctness: never double-debit# Idempotency key from the client (Idempotency-Key header). The payment service stores the key with the request hash and the final response. A retry returns the same result. Payment state machine persisted in the payment DB: RECEIVED → VALIDATED → FUNDS_RESERVED → SUBMITTED → SETTLED | REJECTED | TIMED_OUT. Each transition is a local ACID transaction. Transactional outbox: every state change writes an outbox row in the same transaction. Debezium publishes it to Kafka. See outbox and CDC. Ledger is double-entry and append-only. Postings are idempotent on (paymentId, leg), so a replay cannot post twice. Scheme timeouts: when the scheme does not answer in time, the payment moves to TIMED_OUT. An investigation and status query flow resolves it. Never blindly retry a submission without the scheme&rsquo;s own idempotency reference. 5. Fraud in the stream# A Flink job maintains per-card and per-account features (velocity, amount z-score, new payee, device change, geo) in event-time windows. It writes them to a low-latency store. The payment service calls the fraud decision service synchronously. That service reads the precomputed features and scores them with a model under a 50 ms budget, returning approve, step-up (extra SCA) or block. The decision and its explanation are published as events for case management and model feedback. 6. Notifications, reconciliation, analytics# Notifications consume lifecycle events through a share group, which scales beyond the partition count. They are idempotent on (paymentId, status, channel). Reconciliation compares scheme settlement files or messages with ledger postings in a daily batch, plus a streaming intra-day check. Breaks open cases. Analytics: a Kafka Connect Iceberg sink loads events into the lakehouse bronze layer. See data platforms. 7. Multi-region and DR# Component Approach Ledger DB Synchronous replication within the region (3 AZs). Cross-region uses a distributed SQL database (for example CockroachDB, YugabyteDB or Spanner) or async replication with an RPO-tested failover. Kafka One cluster per region. Cluster Linking or MirrorMaker 2 for DR; producers fail over with the region. Payment service Active-active per region, with home-region pinning per account, so one account&rsquo;s payments are processed in one region at a time. Failover Tested quarterly (DORA requires testing). Runbooks automated. 8. Security and compliance# mTLS between services; OAuth 2.0 / FAPI 2.0 profiles for external APIs; SCA at initiation. Tokenised account and card data. Field-level encryption for sensitive fields in events. Kafka ACLs per service principal. Immutable audit trail: the lifecycle topic plus ledger plus logs, sent to a SIEM. DORA major-incident classification and reporting runbooks. See FinTech regulations. 9. Trade-offs# Decision Benefit Cost Synchronous critical path, asynchronous rest Low latency and decoupled side effects Two consistency models to explain Outbox + CDC Atomic state and event Debezium to operate Precomputed fraud features Fast decisions Feature freshness is eventual (seconds) Home-region pinning No cross-region conflicts Failover must move account ownership Common mistakes# Common mistakePutting the whole flow on async events The customer needs an answer within seconds. Keep the critical path synchronous and short. Common mistakeRetrying scheme

b: Purpose# The Data, Distributed Systems &amp; Cybersecurity Knowledge Hub explains event streaming, distributed data consistency, data platforms and security architecture simply, with diagrams and flows. It is written for architects, senior engineers, data engineers and security engineers, especially those working in financial services. It is a companion to the Java &amp; Software Architecture Knowledge Hub, the Enterprise AI &amp; Agentic AI Knowledge Hub and the Cloud Native &amp; Platform Engineering Knowledge Hub. Structure# Kafka, Event-Driven Systems &amp; Stream Processing Distributed Transactions, CQRS, Saga &amp; Consistency Data Platforms, Governance &amp; Data Security Threat Modelling, AI Security &amp; FinTech Regulations Self Review &amp; Quick Check Conventions# Every article has a simple definition, the problem, core concepts with diagrams and flows, practical guidance, common mistakes, a quick check with answers, a summary and references. Key flows are interactive diagrams drawn with Archify. Smaller diagrams are Mermaid, kept in version control next to the text. Versions and currency# Content was reviewed on 1 November 2026. Versions it was checked against include: Streaming: Apache Kafka 4.2 (KRaft only, share groups GA) and Apache Flink 2.2. Data: Apache Iceberg format v3. b: Definitions are deliberately short. Follow the links for the full explanations. A–C# ABAC (attribute-based access control) Access decisions from attributes of the user, the data and the context. See Data security. At-least-once delivery Messages are never lost but may be duplicated. See Producers and consumers. BCBS 239 Basel principles for risk data aggregation and reporting. See Data governance. BOLA Broken object-level authorisation, the top API security risk. See Security architecture. CAP theorem Under a network partition, choose consistency or availability. See Consistency. CDC (change data capture) Streaming database changes from the transaction log. See Outbox and CDC. CDE (cardholder data environment) Systems that store, process or transmit card data, and so fall in PCI DSS scope. See FinTech regulations. Compensating transaction A business action that semantically undoes an earlier saga step. See Saga. Consumer group Kafka consumers sharing partitions, one owner per partition. See Kafka architecture. CQRS Separate models for commands (writes) and queries (reads). See CQRS and event sourcing. Crypto-shredding Making data unreadable by deleting its encryption key. See Data security. D–I# Data contract A producer–consumer agreement covering schema, semantics, quality, SLOs and ownership. See Schemas and contracts. Data mesh Domain-owned data products on a self-serve platform with federated governance. See Data platforms. DORA The EU Digital Operational Resilience Act for financial entities, applicable since January 2025. See FinTech regulations. DPDP Act India&rsquo;s Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023, with Rules notified in 2025. See FinTech regulations. Envelope encryption Data encrypted with a data key, and the data key encrypted with a master key in a KMS or HSM. See Data security. Event sourcing Storing state as an append-only sequence of events. See CQRS and event sourcing. Excessive agency An AI system with more tools, permissions or autonomy than it needs. See AI security. FAPI 2.0 OpenID Foundation security profile for financial-grade APIs. See Security architecture. Iceberg An open table format adding ACID, schema evolution and time travel to files. See Data platforms. Idempotency An operation that has the same effect whether applied once or many times. See Outbox and idempotency. ISR (in-sync replicas) Kafka replicas caught up with the partition leader. See Kafka architecture. K–P# KRaft Kafka&rsquo;s built-in Raft metadata quorum, replacing ZooKeeper since 4.0. See Kafka architecture. Lakehouse Open table formats on object storage, queried by many engines under one catalog. See Data platforms. Lineage The record of where data came from and how it was transformed. See Data governance. LINDDUN A privacy threat-modelling method. See Threat modelling. Linearizability The strongest single-object consistency: behaves like one copy in real-time order. See Consistency. Medallion architecture Bronze (raw), silver (conformed) and gold (product) data layers. See Data platforms. MITRE ATLAS A knowledge base of adversarial techniques against AI systems. See AI security. Outbox pattern Writing state and event in one local transaction, and relaying the event later. See Outbox. PACELC Partition: availability or consistency; else: latency or consistency. See Consistency. PCI DSS The security standard for cardholder data; v4.0.1 is current. See FinTech regulations. Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) Algorithms resistant to quantum attacks (ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA). See Security architecture. Prompt injection Instructions in input or content that manipulate an LLM. See AI security. R–Z# Raft A consensus protocol using leader election and majority log replication. See Consistency. Saga A sequence of local transactions with compensations. See Saga. SBOM A software bill of materials: an inventory of components. See Security architecture. SCA (strong customer authentication) Two of knowledge, possession and inherence, required by PSD2. See FinTech regulations. Schema registry A service that stores schema versions and enforces compatibility. See Schemas and contracts. Share group Queue-style Kafka consumption with per-record acknowledgement (KIP-932). See Kafka architecture. SLSA Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts: build integrity and provenance. See Security architecture. STRIDE Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege. See Threat modelling. TCC (Try–Confirm–Cancel) Reserve resources, then confirm or cancel them. See Distributed transactions. Tokenisation Replacing sensitive values with random tokens mapped in a secure vault. See Data security. Watermark A stream processor&rsquo;s estimate of event-time progress, used to close windows. See Stream processing. Zero trust No implicit trust from network location; verify every request. See Security architecture.
